supino_reto_smith.html:
The bar runs on a fixed vertical track, which removes the job of keeping it balanced and hands those reps back to the chest. This is the press you have actually done — ten sessions in ABC+D1 against zero for the free-weight barbell bench across the ten programs that prescribed it. The fixed path also lets you press with your feet up or your torso shifted without the bar wandering, which is why the Smith is the usual home for pause work and pin work.

Hits: The lower and middle pectoral fibres do the bulk of it, with the front deltoid and the triceps sharing the lockout. Because the track is vertical rather than following a natural arc, the front delt takes slightly more than it would on a barbell.

Purpose: Heavy horizontal pressing without a spotter and without spending reps on stabilisation. It is the movement that sets your pressing load for the block, which is why it takes the warm-up sets and the eighty-second rest.

Swap with: Barbell bench press is the closest match and adds the stabiliser demand back — expect to drop ten to fifteen percent. Machine chest press if the shoulder is irritated, since the handles let you pick your own path. Dumbbell bench press if you want the stretch at the bottom, but it costs you top-end load.

Watch: The fixed track will let you press in a line your shoulder does not like. Set the bench so the bar touches the lower chest, not the collarbone, and do not let the elbows flare to ninety degrees at the bottom.

supino_reto.html:
The most prescribed chest movement in your entire history and the one you have never once logged. It appears in ABC01, ABC02, ABC04 and six of the ABCD blocks, always as the first movement of push day, always with two warm-up sets and the longest rest in the session. In ABC02 it became a four-rung pyramid — twelve to fifteen, ten to twelve, eight to ten, five to eight — the first time any program asked you for a set under eight reps.

Hits: Lower and mid pec as the primary, with the front delt and triceps taking a real share. The free bar also loads the rotator cuff and the serratus as stabilisers in a way no machine does.

Purpose: The reference lift. Its job in a program is to be the number that tells you whether the block worked, which is why it always sits first and always gets the warm-ups. Every other chest movement in the session is arranged around it.

Swap with: Smith bench press is what you have actually been doing and it is a legitimate swap — you keep the pattern and the load, you lose the stabilisation. Dumbbell bench press keeps the free-weight demand and adds range. Machine chest press is the last resort; it keeps the pattern and loses most of what makes the lift a reference.

Watch: Elbows tucked to about sixty degrees from the torso rather than flared square. Bar to the lower chest. If the shoulder complains at the bottom, shorten the range before you reduce the weight.

descending_pin_press.html:
You press from a dead stop off pins set part-way up, and the pins get lower as the sets progress — so each set starts from a slightly longer range than the one before. Your top load here is a hundred and ninety-five pounds against a hundred and fifty on the full-range Smith press, which is the whole point: a shortened range lets you handle a load your full range cannot yet support, and the dead start removes any help from the stretch at the bottom.

Hits: Mid pec and triceps carry the work, and the triceps share is higher than a normal press because the hardest part of a pin press sits above the sticking point where the arms are already partly extended. Dead-stop starting also loads the front delt hard for the first inch.

Purpose: Overload. This is your ABC+D2 intensification answer to a press that had stopped producing new numbers — same pattern, more weight, less range. The descending element means one exercise covers three different ranges across the session.

Swap with: Board press or a plain pin press at a fixed height if the descending setup is too fiddly. Floor press gives you a similar hard stop with no rack work at all. Paused bench press if what you want is the dead start rather than the overload.

Watch: The dead start is where people jerk the shoulder. Set the tension before the bar leaves the pins and press rather than bounce. Do not chase the descending pins down into a range your shoulder has not earned.

supino_reto_com_halteres.html:
Two independent weights, which means each arm travels its own path and the hands can come closer together at the top than a bar allows. That extra few inches of adduction at the top is real chest work that a barbell simply cannot give you. It appears as the fourth chest movement in ABC01 and ABC05 — not the heavy press, but the one that finishes the job the heavy press started.

Hits: Mid and lower pec, with a longer stretch at the bottom than a barbell because nothing stops the hands at chest level. The front delt and triceps assist, and the rotator cuff works hard to control two separate weights.

Purpose: Range and symmetry. In a program that already has a barbell or Smith press, the dumbbell version exists to cover the part of the movement the bar cuts off, and to stop a strong side from carrying a weak one.

Swap with: Flat dumbbell fly if you want even more of the adduction and less of the press. Machine chest press keeps it easy on the shoulders. Hex press — dumbbells pressed together throughout — is the most chest-biased version of this pattern you have logged.

Watch: Getting heavy dumbbells into position is where shoulders get hurt. Sit, place them on your thighs, and kick back one at a time. Do not bring them so low at the bottom that the shoulder rolls forward.

supino_maquina.html:
A seated press with a fixed handle path and your back supported. It shows up in ABCD03, ABCD07, ABCD08 and ABCD11, and in every case it sits after a free-weight press rather than before one. That ordering is the whole prescription: the machine is there to take the chest past the point where your stabilisers would have quit first.

Hits: Mid pec almost exclusively, with a modest triceps and front delt share. The back support removes the trunk from the equation entirely, which is exactly why the chest can be driven closer to failure safely.

Purpose: Safe accumulation of pressing volume. When a program wants four chest movements, the fourth cannot be another free-weight press without wrecking the session — so it becomes a machine.

Swap with: Hammer strength press if your gym has one, since the independent arms add the adduction back. Smith bench press if the machine is taken. Push-ups to failure is the zero-equipment version and covers the same “finish the chest” job.

Watch: Set the seat so the handles line up with your mid chest, not your shoulders. Do not let the weight stack slam — the fixed path makes it easy to use momentum and never notice.

reverse_grip_bench_press_smith_machine.pt: Reverse Grip Bench Press Smith Machine
reverse_grip_bench_press_smith_machine.html:
Press a flat bar with your palms facing you. Turning the grip over rotates the upper arm in a way that shifts a surprising amount of the work onto the upper chest — enough that a flat reverse-grip press loads the clavicular fibres about as well as a modest incline does. It appeared in ABCD09 as the second press of the day, right after dumbbell circles and before dips.

Hits: Upper pec more than any other flat press, with the front delt and the long head of the triceps assisting. The supinated grip also brings the biceps in as a stabiliser, which no other press does.

Purpose: Upper-chest loading without an incline bench, and a genuinely different stimulus in a block that was already running an incline press elsewhere. ABCD09 was an accumulation block with only ten percent carry-over — novelty was the point.

Swap with: Incline Smith bench for the same upper-chest target through a more conventional path. Reverse grip barbell bench if you want it free-weight, though unracking it safely needs a spotter. Low-incline press at fifteen to twenty degrees gets you most of the way.

Watch: The grip is the hazard, not the press. Wrists will want to collapse backward under load; keep them stacked. On a Smith this is manageable, with a free bar it is genuinely risky.

supino_inclinado_smith_30_37.html:
Your most-logged chest press, and the one place where your own programs went further than your trainer's ever did: ABC+D1 and ABC+D3 specify the bench angle in degrees rather than just calling it “incline.” That matters more than it sounds. At thirty degrees the upper chest does most of the work; by forty-five the front delt has quietly taken over, and by sixty you are doing a shoulder press with a chest stretch. Thirty to thirty-seven is the window where the clavicular pec is loaded and the delt is still only helping.

Hits: Upper pec as the primary, front delt and triceps assisting, with the mid pec contributing through the bottom half of the range. The fixed bar path keeps the load travelling straight up, which keeps the emphasis honest.

Purpose: Upper-chest thickness, loaded heavily and repeatably. It is the movement that carries your pressing progression in the ABC+D blocks the way barbell bench was meant to in your trainer's.

Swap with: Incline dumbbell press for more range and a harder stabilisation demand, at a lower load. Incline barbell press if you want the free-weight version. Reverse grip flat Smith press reaches similar fibres from a completely different angle if the incline bench is occupied.

Watch: Creeping the bench angle up over a block without noticing. If the front delts are the thing that fatigues first, the bench is too steep. Keep the bar touching high on the chest, not on the throat.

supino_inclinado_com_halteres.html:
The single most-prescribed chest movement across your whole history — fourteen of nineteen programs — and it survived every transition your trainer made. It is in ABC03 and ABC04, in all eight ABCD blocks from 01 to 08, in ABCD10 and ABCD11, and in your own ABC+D2 and ABC+D3. When a coach keeps one movement through four different training philosophies, that is a vote of confidence.

Hits: Upper pec primary, with a meaningfully larger front-delt share than the Smith version because the dumbbells let the arms travel inward at the top. The stretch at the bottom is deeper than any barred press can give you.

Purpose: Upper chest with range. In programs that already have a heavy barred press, this is the second press — the one that covers the adduction and the deep stretch the bar cuts off. In ABC03's specialization block it was the third incline movement in a row, the point at which the block openly admitted it was an upper-chest specialisation.

Swap with: Incline Smith press for more load and less range. Neutral grip incline dumbbell press if the shoulder complains — palms facing each other is the friendliest version of this movement. Incline dumbbell fly if what you want is purely the adduction.

Watch: Bringing the dumbbells together hard at the top costs you nothing and gains you the best part of the rep, but clanging them together turns it into a rest. Control the bottom; this is the position where an incline press hurts a shoulder.

supino_inclinado.html:
The free-weight incline. In ABC03 it led push day at four sets of eight to ten — the first time a program put an incline movement first rather than treating it as the follow-up to a flat press. That reordering was the clearest signal in the whole ABC series that the block was specialising the upper chest.

Hits: Upper pec primary, front delt and triceps assisting, with the stabilisers working harder than on a Smith.

Purpose: Heavy upper-chest pressing that also counts as a reference lift. When it leads the day, the program is telling you the upper chest is the priority for the block.

Swap with: Incline Smith press for the same path with less balance cost. Incline dumbbell press for range. Low-incline guillotine press if you want maximum upper pec and are willing to go very light.

Watch: Unracking an incline barbell is awkward and is where shoulders get tweaked. Get help or use a rack with the pins set high.

supino_maquina_inclinado.html:
The second movement of push day in both ABC01 and ABC02, sitting directly behind barbell bench at four sets of eight to twelve with eighty seconds rest. Its job in that slot is to keep pressing the upper chest after the free-weight lift has already used up your stability.

Hits: Upper pec, with the back support removing the trunk entirely and the fixed path keeping the front delt's share lower than a free incline would.

Purpose: Upper-chest volume that costs the nervous system almost nothing, immediately after a lift that cost it a lot.

Swap with: Incline Smith press is the nearest thing with a fixed path. Incline dumbbell press if you will accept the extra stabilisation. Incline seated cable fly if the goal is just more upper-chest work without more pressing.

Watch: Seat height. If the handles sit above your shoulders the movement becomes a shoulder press with extra steps.

supino_declinado_smith.html:
Head below hips, bar travelling from the lower chest outward. The decline angle shortens the range and takes the front delt almost entirely out of the movement, which is why the load matches your flat Smith press despite the shorter path. It appeared in ABC+D2 as one of three distinct pressing angles in the same block.

Hits: Lower pec, more cleanly isolated than any other press, with the triceps assisting. The front delt's contribution is the lowest of any pressing movement here, which is the whole argument for including it.

Purpose: Lower-chest work and a pressing pattern that gives the front delts a rest. In a block that already has flat and incline pressing, decline is the third angle that adds stimulus without adding shoulder wear.

Swap with: Weighted dips is the closest functional match and needs no bench at all. High-to-low cable fly for the same fibres with no pressing. Decline machine press if the Smith is in use.

Watch: Getting in and out of a decline bench under load. Set up, then have the bar handed to you or use the pins. People with blood-pressure issues should skip the head-down position entirely.

paralela.html:
The only chest press where you move your body instead of the weight, and the angle of your torso decides what it trains. Lean forward with the elbows flared and it is a lower-chest press; stay upright with the elbows tucked and it becomes one of the best triceps movements there is. Your programs treat it as a chest movement — it sits in the chest block in ABCD04, 06, 08, 09, 10 and 11, usually second or third in the session with a hundred and twenty seconds rest.

Hits: Lower pec and triceps roughly evenly, with the front delt taking a real share at the bottom. As shown here the figure reflects the chest-biased forward-lean version your programs prescribe.

Purpose: Heavy lower-chest and triceps pressing with a deep stretch at the bottom that no barred movement reproduces. It also loads the pattern with your own bodyweight, which is why it carries across six programs without needing a machine.

Swap with: Decline Smith or decline machine press for the same fibres with the range controlled. Dip machine or assisted dip if the bodyweight version is too much. Gironda dip — extreme forward lean, wide elbows — if you want maximum chest and minimum triceps.

Watch: The bottom. Descending until the shoulders roll forward past the elbows is the most reliable way to injure a shoulder in this atlas. Stop when the upper arm is roughly parallel to the floor and earn depth slowly.

apoio_flexao.html:
In ABC02 these were bi-set with the machine fly and taken to failure — which tells you exactly what they were for. Nobody puts push-ups after a machine fly for strength. They are there because they cost nothing to set up, they can be taken all the way to failure without risk, and the fly has already pre-exhausted the chest so a bodyweight movement is genuinely hard.

Hits: Mid pec, triceps and front delt, plus real isometric work from the abs and obliques holding the plank — a contribution no bench press makes.

Purpose: Failure work at the end of a chest block, with zero equipment and zero risk. When a program wants you to find the true end of a set, this is the safest place to do it.

Swap with: Machine chest press to failure if you want the load controlled. Weighted push-ups once bodyweight stops being difficult. Serratus dip or deficit push-up on handles to get more range.

Watch: The hips sagging as fatigue arrives. The moment the plank breaks, the movement stops being chest work and becomes lower-back work.

weighted_push_ups.html:
A push-up with a plate on your back, opening ABC+D1's upper day with two warm-up sets and four working sets of eight to twelve. Putting a loaded push-up first in a session rather than last is an unusual choice and a defensible one — it warms the shoulder through a full range under moderate load before anything heavy happens.

Hits: Mid pec, triceps, front delt, with the core working harder than in an unloaded push-up because the plate wants to fold you in half.

Purpose: Loaded pressing that doubles as a shoulder warm-up. It fills the first slot of a day without committing the joint to a heavy barred lift cold.

Swap with: Push-ups plain if there is nobody to load your back. Machine chest press for the same early-session volume with easier loading. Dumbbell bench press if you want a real first press.

Watch: Plate placement — it belongs between the shoulder blades, not on the lower back, and you need someone to set it. Do not let the added load pull the hips into a sag.

supino_maquina_declinado.html:
Added in ABC02 purely so that push day had five distinct chest lines. That is the honest reason — the intensification block kept the volume flat and made each set cost more, and a fifth pressing angle was part of how it filled the sheet without adding another heavy lift.

Hits: Lower pec with triceps support, back supported, front delt largely absent.

Purpose: A fifth chest angle at near-zero cost to recovery. Decline is the angle you add when flat and incline are already taken.

Swap with: Weighted dips, decline Smith press, or high-to-low cable fly — any of the three covers the lower chest better than this does.

Watch: Nothing much; it is a machine on a short range. The risk is spending a slot on it that a dip would use better.

crucifixo_halter_flat_dumbell_fly_p_flat.html:
Arms nearly straight, opening wide and closing in an arc. Logged under two names in your app — the Portuguese in the ABC+D blocks and the English in ABCD09 — which together make it your most-used chest isolation movement by a wide margin. The defining property of a dumbbell fly is that gravity pulls straight down, so the movement is hardest at the bottom where the chest is stretched and almost free at the top where the hands meet. That is the opposite of a cable fly and the reason a program can justify running both.

Hits: Mid pec through a very long stretch, with the front delt assisting and the biceps working isometrically to hold the elbow angle. No triceps involvement at all, which is what separates a fly from a press.

Purpose: Chest work with the triceps removed. After two presses the triceps are usually the limiting factor; a fly lets you keep loading the chest once that is true. The deep stretch at the bottom is also the single best thing this movement offers.

Swap with: Cable fly keeps tension at the top where dumbbells lose it — a genuine upgrade if a cable station is free. Chest fly machine for a fixed path and easy failure work. Pec deck or dumbbell fly on the floor if the bottom position bothers your shoulder, since the floor caps the stretch.

Watch: Going too heavy turns a fly into a bad press — if the elbows are bending to move the weight, it is too much. The bottom is a real shoulder position; lower under control and do not bounce out of the stretch.

crucifixo_na_polia.html:
The most widely prescribed fly in your history — eleven programs, from ABC01 all the way through ABCD08 — and the one where the resistance profile actually favours the part of the movement that matters. A cable pulls horizontally, so tension stays on the chest right through to the point where your hands meet, which is exactly where a dumbbell fly gives up. In ABC02 it picked up rest-pause work, which only makes sense on a movement that keeps loading the muscle at the finish.

Hits: Mid pec, with the emphasis sliding toward the upper or lower fibres depending on whether the cables are set low, level, or high. Front delt assists throughout.

Purpose: Constant-tension chest isolation and the natural home for fatigue techniques — rest-pause, drop sets, twenty-one style partials — because the cable never lets the muscle rest mid-rep.

Swap with: Chest fly machine for the same constant tension with less setup. Flat dumbbell fly if the cables are busy, accepting that you trade top-end tension for bottom-end stretch. Cable crossover if you want to exaggerate the squeeze past the midline.

Watch: Pulley height changes the exercise, so pick one and keep it for the block rather than drifting. Keep a soft fixed bend in the elbow; straightening and rebending it mid-rep turns this into a triceps movement.

incline_seated_cable_fly_37.html:
A bench set at thirty-seven degrees between two low pulleys, so the cables pull down and out while you fly up and in. It is the cleanest upper-chest isolation available — incline angle for the fibre bias, cable resistance for tension at the top — and it sits second in ABC+D1's push day, right behind the Smith bench.

Hits: Upper pec almost alone, with the front delt assisting. Putting an isolation movement this early in a session is deliberate: the upper chest gets attention while it is still fresh.

Purpose: Upper-chest isolation with constant tension. In a block where the main press is flat, this is what keeps the clavicular fibres in the program.

Swap with: Incline dumbbell fly for the free-weight version with a better stretch and a worse top. Low-to-high cable fly standing, which is nearly the same movement without the bench. Incline fly with crossover if you want the extra squeeze past the midline.

Watch: Bench angle drift and pulley height are both easy to get wrong week to week; note the settings. Keep the shoulder blades pinned to the bench so the delt does not take over.

incline_fly_with_crossover_p_squeeze_p.html:
An incline fly where the hands do not stop when they meet — they cross, one over the other, and hold the squeeze. Crossing past the midline is the only way to fully shorten the pectoral, because the muscle's job is pulling the arm across the body and a normal fly stops half way through that job. The light top load of seventeen and a half pounds is not a weakness; it is what the movement is worth when done properly.

Hits: Upper and inner pec, taken through the shortest position the muscle can reach. Front delt assists. Alternating which hand crosses on top each rep keeps it even.

Purpose: Peak contraction. Its entire reason for existing is the last three inches of the movement, which nothing else in a chest session reaches.

Swap with: Cable crossover standing, which does the same thing with better resistance. Incline seated cable fly if you would rather have constant tension than the cross. Pec deck with a hold at the finish.

Watch: The temptation to add weight. This movement rewards a hard two-second squeeze at a weight that looks embarrassing; loading it heavier just removes the cross.

crucifixo_inclinado_com_halteres.html:
The second of ABC03's three consecutive incline movements — incline barbell, then incline dumbbell flyes, then an incline dumbbell press pyramid. Three incline lines in a row is not variety, it is a declaration that the block was specialising the upper chest, and the fly in the middle is what stops the sequence from being three presses.

Hits: Upper pec through a deep stretch, front delt assisting, no triceps.

Purpose: Upper-chest stretch between two upper chest presses, giving the triceps a break without giving the chest one.

Swap with: Incline seated cable fly for tension at the top. Flat dumbbell fly if the incline benches are taken. Incline fly with crossover for the squeeze.

Watch: The bottom of an incline fly is the deepest shoulder stretch in a chest session. Go light, go slow, and stop when the shoulder rather than the chest is what you feel.

crucifixo_p_voador_p.html:
Prescribed in six programs — ABC02, ABC03, ABC04, ABCD01, ABCD04, ABCD06 — and in ABC02 it was the movement bi-set with push-ups to failure. Its value is that the path is fixed and your back is supported, so you can go to genuine failure on a chest isolation movement without any of the setup risk a dumbbell fly carries.

Hits: Mid pec, hardest through the middle of the arc rather than at either end. Front delt assists modestly.

Purpose: Failure-safe chest isolation. It is the default home for drop sets, bi-sets and rest-pause because nothing can go wrong when the weight runs out.

Swap with: Cable fly for a better resistance curve at the expense of stability. Flat dumbbell fly if no machine exists. Pec deck is the same movement under another name.

Watch: Seat height — the handles should sit at chest level, not shoulder level. Letting the stack touch down between reps gives the chest a rest it has not earned.

dumbell_circles.hits: Front and side delt, rotator cuff
dumbell_circles.html:
Filed under chest in the app, but it is not a chest movement — it is the warm-up that opens push day in ABC+D2, ABC+D3 and ABCD09. Light dumbbells taken through full circles at the shoulder, four sets of twelve at five pounds, twenty-five logged sessions. It is the third most-logged movement in your entire history after the two shoulder rotations, and it belongs to the same family: cheap work done before the heavy work that keeps the joint healthy.

Hits: The whole deltoid and the rotator cuff through a full range, with the upper pec and traps along for the ride. Nothing here is being trained for size; it is being prepared.

Purpose: Getting blood and range into the shoulder before a pressing session. The reason it appears in exactly the three blocks that press heaviest is not a coincidence.

Swap with: Arm circles unloaded, or band pull-aparts, or shoulder dislocates with a broomstick — any general shoulder prep covers this. Internal and external rotations if you want the cuff work specifically rather than general range.

Watch: The weight. Five pounds is correct; this is not a lateral raise and making it heavy defeats the purpose.

supino_maquina_hammer.html:
A Hammer Strength-style plate-loaded press with independent converging arms. The independence is what separates it from a cable-stack machine: each arm moves on its own, and the handles travel inward as they extend, so you get the adduction at the top that a barbell cannot give. Two hundred and forty-five pounds is your heaviest logged chest load, which is what a well-designed machine buys you.

Hits: Mid pec with the converging path adding real adduction at lockout, front delt and triceps assisting, trunk entirely supported.

Purpose: Heavy pressing with dumbbell-style convergence and machine-style safety. It is the best of both, which is why it is worth seeking out when a gym has one.

Swap with: Machine chest press on a standard converging machine. Smith bench press for a barred fixed path. Dumbbell bench press for the free-weight version of the convergence.

Watch: Seat height, as with every chest machine — handles at mid-chest. The independent arms will also let a stronger side do more without you noticing, so watch that both sides finish together.

hex_press_smith.html:
A press with the hands squeezed together throughout the rep — normally done with two dumbbells pressed against each other, here run on the Smith. Keeping the hands pinned together means the pecs are contracting to hold the weights in as well as to press them up, so the chest is loaded isometrically and dynamically at the same time. That is why it is the most chest-biased press in the section.

Hits: Inner and mid pec, with the triceps and front delt assisting. The constant squeeze is what shifts emphasis away from the delt.

Purpose: A press that behaves like a fly. When a session wants more chest and less shoulder from its pressing, this is the variation that delivers it.

Swap with: Hex press with dumbbells, which is the standard version. Close grip bench press for a similar inner-chest emphasis. Cable fly if the squeeze is what you are after.

Watch: Losing the squeeze as the set gets hard, at which point it becomes an ordinary narrow press. If the hands separate, the set is done.

crucifixo_na_maquina_crucifixo_voador_p_.html:
The pec deck, logged under two names depending on which floor of the gym the machine was on. The fixed arc and supported back make it the easiest place in a chest session to go to genuine failure, and the hundred-and-forty-five-pound load reflects how much a machine's leverage flatters a fly.

Hits: Mid pec, hardest through the middle of the arc, front delt assisting modestly.

Purpose: Failure-safe chest isolation. It is the same role the chest fly machine plays across the six programs that prescribe it — the home for drop sets and bi-sets.

Swap with: Chest fly machine — the same thing. Cable fly for a better resistance curve. Flat dumbbell fly for the stretch.

Watch: Setting the start position so wide that the shoulder is stretched before the rep begins. Most pec decks have an adjustable start; use it.

puxada.html:
Twelve of nineteen programs, which makes it the most prescribed back movement you have and the one that almost always opens pull day. In ABC01 it takes the warm-up sets and the eighty-second rest — the same treatment barbell bench gets on push day — and in ABC03 it became a pyramid. Its advantage over a pull-up is simply that you can load it at any weight, which means it works as a first heavy movement whether you are strong that week or not.

Hits: Lats through their full range, with the biceps taking a real share and the rear delt and mid traps helping at the bottom. A wider grip biases the upper lat and a narrower one lets you pull further.

Purpose: The loadable vertical pull. It sets the pulling number for the block the way a bench press sets the pressing number, and it is adjustable enough to warm up on.

Swap with: Pull-ups if you can do enough reps, since it is the same pattern with a harder stabilisation demand. V-bar pulldown for a longer range and more lower-lat. Single arm pulldown if one side is lagging.

Watch: Leaning back to turn it into a row. A little lean is fine and constant is better than creeping. Pull to the collarbone, not behind the neck.

puxada_frente_triangulo.html:
A close neutral-grip handle instead of a wide bar, which changes the movement more than it looks. The hands travel closer to the body and the elbows come further past the torso, so the lats shorten more completely than a wide pulldown allows. Your top load here is the heaviest of any pulling movement in the atlas at two hundred and three pounds, which tells you the mechanics suit you.

Hits: Lower lat fibres get the biggest share, with the biceps strongly involved because of the neutral grip, and the mid traps at the finish.

Purpose: The longer-range vertical pull. Where a wide pulldown builds width, this reaches the part of the lat closest to the waist. In eleven programs it sits second on pull day, right after the wide pulldown, for exactly that reason.

Swap with: Close grip pulldown or chin-ups, both of which use a similar arm path. Lat pulldown wide if you want width instead of range. Rope lat pulldown for the same path with a free hand position.

Watch: Because it feels strong, it invites heaving. Keep the torso angle fixed and let the elbows drive down and back rather than rocking the whole body.

puxada_frente_triangulo_body_weight.html:
A V-bar pulldown loaded to bodyweight or beyond, so that instead of the bar coming to you, you come to the bar. ABC+D1 ran it second on pull day behind the Yates row, with two warm-up sets. The distinction from a neutral-grip pull-up is the seat: you stay pinned, so the load is pure pulling with none of the swing.

Hits: Lower lats, biceps, and a genuine isometric demand on the core to keep you from being lifted off the seat.

Purpose: Bridging the gap between a pulldown and a weighted pull-up — heavy relative load without needing to hang from a bar.

Swap with: Neutral grip pull-ups for the free-hanging version. V-bar pulldown at sub-bodyweight loads. Weighted chin-ups if the goal is maximum relative strength.

Watch: The thigh pad has to actually hold you down or the movement becomes a partial. Set it before you load the stack.

barra.html:
In ABC02 pull-ups to failure were moved to the front of pull day, replacing the pulldown as the opener. That is a meaningful change: a set to failure at bodyweight is a different test from four sets at a chosen weight, and putting it first means the program wanted to know where you actually were before loading anything.

Hits: Lats primarily, biceps heavily, rear delts at the top, and the whole trunk isometrically because nothing is holding you still.

Purpose: An honest relative-strength benchmark and the vertical pull that cannot be cheated with body english as easily as a pulldown. When a program opens with pull-ups to failure it is using them as a measurement, not just as volume.

Swap with: Lat pulldown if you cannot hit the target reps — same pattern, adjustable load. Assisted pull-up machine or band-assisted pull-ups to bridge. Chin-ups if the pronated grip bothers your elbow.

Watch: Kipping. The moment the hips start generating the rep it stops being a back movement. Full hang at the bottom, chin over the bar at the top, no swing between.

weighted_chin_ups.html:
Palms facing you, with a dip belt. ABCD10 ran it as a four-rung pyramid — twelve, ten, eight, five — opening pull day. The supinated grip puts the biceps in a stronger position than a pull-up does, which is why most people can load a chin heavier than a pull-up and why the biceps get a bigger slice of the work.

Hits: Lats and biceps, closer to evenly split than any other pulling movement here. Core works isometrically against the hanging weight.

Purpose: Loaded vertical pulling that doubles as heavy biceps work. In a program that puts only two biceps movements on pull day, a weighted chin quietly adds a third.

Swap with: Weighted pull-ups for less biceps and more lat. V-bar pulldown heavy, which uses a similar arm path. Close grip pulldown if belt-loading is awkward.

Watch: Elbow tendons. Heavy supinated pulling is the most reliable route to inner-elbow pain in this atlas. Add weight slowly and stop the set before the last rep turns into a struggle.

pull_up_weighted.html:
The pronated twin of the weighted chin, run in ABCD11's peak block. Same load, different grip, and the difference is real: overhand puts the biceps at a mechanical disadvantage, so more of the work lands on the lat and the rear delt. If you are doing both in a training year, this is the one that is more specifically a back movement.

Hits: Lats, with rear delts more involved than in a chin and the biceps less so. Core holds the load steady.

Purpose: Maximum-strength vertical pulling in a peak block, where the point is a low-rep heavy set rather than volume.

Swap with: Weighted chin-ups if the elbow prefers a supinated grip. Lat pulldown heavy at low reps. Neutral grip weighted pull-up as the middle ground between the two grips.

Watch: Shoulder position at the dead hang with added weight. Keep a little tension in the upper back at the bottom rather than hanging completely slack.

single_arm_pulldown_with_bend.html:
One arm at a time with a deliberate lean away from the working side, which opens up more range than any two-handed pulldown can reach. The bend is the point: leaning lets the lat start from a fully lengthened position and finish fully shortened, covering a range a bar physically blocks. ABC+D1 ran it for seven sessions and twenty-six sets.

Hits: One lat through its longest available range, with the biceps assisting and the obliques working hard on the opposite side to control the lean.

Purpose: Range and symmetry. It is the movement that finds the part of the lat two-handed work cannot, and it exposes a side-to-side difference that a bar would hide.

Swap with: One-arm lat pulldown without the lean if the obliques are the limiting factor. Kneeling single-arm cable pulldown for more stability. One-arm DB row if you want unilateral back work in the horizontal plane instead.

Watch: Rotating rather than side-bending. The torso should hinge sideways, not twist, or the lat loses the line of pull entirely.

barra_pegada_inversa.html:
The unweighted supinated pull-up, prescribed once in ABC04's realization block. In a block that cut eight exercises to let the remaining ones go heavy, a bodyweight chin is a sensible way to keep a vertical pull in the program without adding another loaded lift.

Hits: Lats and biceps, with the biceps share higher than a pronated pull-up because of the grip.

Purpose: Vertical pulling volume at zero setup cost in a stripped-down block.

Swap with: Pull-ups for less biceps, weighted chin-ups once bodyweight is easy, or V-bar pulldown for the same arm path with adjustable load.

Watch: Inner elbow. Supinated pulling at high volume is where that tendon complains first.

puxada_pegada_inversa.html:
A pulldown with the palms facing you. Turning the grip over draws the elbows in tight to the ribs, which shortens the lat more completely than a wide overhand grip and shifts the emphasis toward the lower fibres. It is the seated, loadable equivalent of a chin-up.

Hits: Lower lats with substantial biceps involvement.

Purpose: Lower-lat emphasis with adjustable load — useful when you want the chin-up stimulus but need to control the weight precisely.

Swap with: V-bar pulldown for a similar elbow path with a neutral grip that is kinder to the wrist. Chin-ups for the bodyweight version. Supinated wide grip pulldown as a variation.

Watch: Wrist and elbow strain from the supinated grip under load. If either complains, switch to the neutral V-bar.

remada_curvada_com_barra.html:
Eleven programs prescribed it and you have one logged session. That makes it the back mirror of barbell bench press — the movement your trainer trusted most and the one you consistently replaced with something else, usually a Yates row, a T-bar or a Smith row. In ABC02 it was an ascending pyramid; in most others it sits fourth on pull day after the pulldowns.

Hits: The widest spread of any back movement: lats, rhomboids and mid traps all take real work, with the biceps and rear delts assisting and the erectors working hard isometrically to hold the torso over. That last part is the movement's cost and its value.

Purpose: The reference horizontal pull. Nothing else loads the mid-back and the spinal erectors together like an unsupported bent-over row, which is exactly why a coach keeps putting it in and exactly why it is the first thing to get swapped when the lower back is tired.

Swap with: Yates row keeps the barbell and the load while reducing the erector demand through a more upright torso. T-bar row or chest-supported row removes the lower back entirely. One-arm DB row if you want unilateral work and a braced torso.

Watch: The back rounding as the set goes on. Fix the torso angle before the first rep and treat any change in it as the end of the set. Pull to the navel, not the chest.

yates_row.html:
An underhand barbell row with the torso much more upright than a classic bent-over row — around forty-five degrees rather than parallel to the floor. Dorian Yates built his back on it, and the trade is explicit: you give up some lat range in exchange for a position you can load far heavier and hold safely. You opened ABC+D1's pull day with it at a hundred and sixty pounds, more than your logged bent-over row by half again.

Hits: Lats and mid traps, with the supinated grip bringing the biceps in strongly. The more upright torso means the erectors work considerably less than in a true bent-over row.

Purpose: Heavy horizontal pulling that does not tax the lower back enough to compromise the rest of the session. It is the row you lead with when the day also contains a deficit row and a deadlift pattern.

Swap with: Bent over barbell row if you want the full erector demand back. T-bar row for a similar load with a neutral grip. Pendlay row if you want the dead stop instead of the upright torso.

Watch: Torso angle creeping upward as the weight goes up, at which point it becomes an upright row with extra steps. Pick an angle and hold it across the block.

deficit_remada_curvada_com_barra.html:
Standing on a platform so the bar can travel below where the floor would normally stop it. The extra few inches at the bottom put the lats into a deeper stretch than any standard row reaches, and the load drops accordingly — eighty-five pounds against a hundred and sixty on the Yates row in the same program. That is not weakness, it is the price of the range.

Hits: Lats through an extended stretch, plus rhomboids and mid traps at the top. The erectors work through a longer range than usual, which is what makes it demanding.

Purpose: Stretch under load. ABC+D1 paired it with the Yates row so the day covered both ends of the rowing range — heavy and short from one, light and long from the other.

Swap with: Bent over barbell row from the floor if the deficit is too much for the lower back. Chest supported row with a long range if you want the stretch without the erector cost. Snatch grip deficit row for even more range.

Watch: This is the highest lower-back-risk movement in the back section. The bottom position under a longer lever is exactly where a rounded spine does damage. Go light and stop the set when the position changes.

tbar_row.html:
One end of the bar anchored in a landmine, the other loaded, with a neutral handle. The fixed pivot means the bar travels a predictable arc and you can pull genuinely heavy without the balance problem of a free barbell row. In ABCD09 it sat second on pull day with two warm-up sets and a hundred and twenty seconds rest — treated as a primary lift.

Hits: Lats, rhomboids and mid traps together. The neutral close grip drives the elbows past the torso, which gets a stronger mid-back squeeze than a wide pronated row.

Purpose: Heavy mid-back thickness. It is the compromise row: most of the loading potential of a barbell, most of the stability of a machine.

Swap with: Chest supported row to take the lower back fully out. Bent over barbell row for the unsupported version. Seated cable row with a close handle for the same elbow path seated.

Watch: Standing too upright shortens the range to nothing. Hinge properly, and resist the urge to bounce the plates off the floor between reps.

reeves_row_p_ez_bar_p.html:
Named after Steve Reeves, who rowed by gripping the plates themselves rather than the bar. Your version uses an EZ bar at the widest possible grip, which achieves the same thing: a very wide hand position that pulls the elbows out away from the body and turns a row into a rear-delt and upper-back movement rather than a lat movement. ABCD09 and ABCD10 both ran it, the latter as a pyramid.

Hits: Rear delts and mid traps get the biggest share, with the upper lat assisting. The extreme grip width also makes this genuine forearm and grip work.

Purpose: Upper-back and rear-delt thickness from a rowing pattern. When a program's other rows are all close-grip and lat-biased, this is the one that covers the space between the shoulder blades and the back of the shoulder.

Swap with: Wide grip seated row for the same elbow flare with the torso supported. Rope upright row or face pulls if what you want is purely the rear delt. Kelso shrug for the pure scapular squeeze.

Watch: Grip failing before the back does. If the hands are the limiting factor, straps make this a back exercise again.

helms_row.html:
A chest-supported dumbbell row on a high incline bench, named after Eric Helms. The bench does the job the lower back would otherwise do, so every rep goes to the target muscles and nothing goes to holding you up. The load looks modest at sixty-five pounds precisely because nothing is helping.

Hits: Lats and mid traps with the rear delts involved, and zero erector demand. It is the purest mid-back row in the atlas.

Purpose: Rowing volume with no lower-back cost. This is the row you use late in a session, or in a program that already has a deadlift and a deficit row competing for the same spinal recovery.

Swap with: Chest supported barbell row for more load. Seated cable row for a similar supported feel. Incline close grip row if you want the elbows tighter.

Watch: Lifting the chest off the pad to cheat the last reps. If the chest leaves the bench, the movement has become a standing row and lost its whole point.

smith_machine_row.html:
Rowing the Smith bar on its fixed vertical track while hinged over. The track removes the need to control the bar's path forward and back, so all you manage is the up-and-down — which makes it a bent-over row with the balance problem deleted. ABC+D3 used it as the block's loadable row.

Hits: Lats and mid traps, with the erectors still working to hold the hinge but less than a free barbell demands.

Purpose: Bent-over rowing for someone who wants the pattern without spending attention on bar path. It is the rowing equivalent of choosing the Smith bench over the barbell bench — the same trade you have made consistently for two years.

Swap with: Bent over barbell row for the free version. T-bar row for a similar guided feel with a neutral grip. Smith machine incline row if you want chest support.

Watch: The fixed track will not let the bar follow your natural arc, so stand where the bar meets your navel at the top rather than fighting the path.

remada_curvada_kroc_row.html:
A one-arm dumbbell row taken deliberately heavy and deliberately loose, for high reps, with body english allowed. Janae Kroc popularised it as a grip and back builder where the normal strictness rules are suspended on purpose. ABCD03 prescribed it once.

Hits: Lats and mid traps, with real forearm and grip work from holding a heavy dumbbell for fifteen or twenty reps, and the obliques bracing against rotation.

Purpose: Loading a row heavier than strict form allows, to build grip and give the back a stimulus it does not get from controlled work.

Swap with: One-arm DB row strict, if you would rather not use momentum. Dead stop dumbbell row for a controlled version of the same heavy single-arm idea. Meadows row for a landmine variation.

Watch: This movement intentionally breaks the rules, so it only makes sense if your lower back is healthy and you keep the spine from rounding even while the torso moves. Straps are expected.

remada_unilateral_com_halter.html:
Nine programs and nine logged sessions — one of the very few movements where what was prescribed and what you did line up. One hand and one knee on the bench, the other arm rowing a dumbbell from a full hang to the hip. Bracing on the bench means the lower back is supported while the working side still gets a completely free range of motion, which is a rare combination.

Hits: One lat through a long range, biceps and mid traps assisting, and the obliques working to stop the torso rotating toward the weight. ABC03 ran it as an ascending pyramid.

Purpose: Unilateral back work with a braced torso. It exposes a side-to-side strength difference and lets the stronger arm's range be matched by the weaker one, which a barbell hides completely.

Swap with: Single arm seated row for the same unilateral idea on a cable with constant tension. Meadows row for a landmine version with a different angle of pull. Chest supported dumbbell row if you want both arms supported.

Watch: Rotating the torso to get the dumbbell higher. The shoulders should stay square to the floor; if they twist, the lat has stopped working and the obliques have taken over.

remada_baixa_remada_baixa_triangulo.html:
Ten programs, from ABC02 through ABCD08, almost always in the middle of pull day. The cable keeps tension constant through the whole stroke, which is the one thing a free-weight row cannot do — at the top of a barbell row gravity is pulling straight down while you are pulling straight back, so the load falls away exactly where the mid-back squeeze should be hardest. On a cable it does not. In ABC02 it carried rest-pause work for that reason.

Hits: Lats, rhomboids and mid traps, with the handle choice deciding the balance — a close V-handle biases the lats, a wide bar biases the rhomboids and rear delts.

Purpose: Constant-tension horizontal pulling with the lower back supported. It is the row a program uses for volume and technique work rather than for a maximum.

Swap with: Chest supported row for a similar supported feel with free weights. T-bar row if you want more load. Machine row if the cable station is taken.

Watch: Rocking back and forth from the hips to move the stack. A small lean is acceptable; swinging turns the erectors into the prime mover and the back gets nothing.

remada_baixa_pegada_aberta_supinada.html:
Your most-logged rowing movement, run across ABC+D2 and ABC+D3. A wide grip with the palms turned up is an unusual combination — wide grips normally go with a pronated hand — and it produces an elbow path that stays close to the body while the hands stay far apart. The result loads the lower lat hard while still getting a scapular squeeze at the end.

Hits: Lower lats primarily, with the biceps in a strong position because of the supinated grip, and the mid traps finishing the rep.

Purpose: The lat-biased row in a program whose other rows are mid-back biased. Across two of your own blocks it did the job that the bent-over row does in your trainer's.

Swap with: Seated cable row with a close neutral handle for a similar lat bias. Reverse grip triangle row for the same grip idea narrower. Yates row for the free-weight equivalent.

Watch: Wrist position. A wide supinated grip puts the wrist in an awkward spot under load; an EZ-style cambered handle solves it if your gym has one.

cable_row_with_rope.html:
A rope instead of a bar, which means the hands are not locked to a fixed width and can pull apart at the finish. That single freedom changes the movement: the elbows can flare and travel further back than any handle permits, and the rep ends with the shoulder blades fully squeezed rather than wherever the bar stops them.

Hits: Mid traps, rhomboids and rear delts more than the lats, because the elbow path is high and wide rather than tight to the ribs.

Purpose: Upper-back detail work. In ABCD11's peak block, where most movements were heavy and short, this was the one that covered the squeeze.

Swap with: Face pulls for an even more rear-delt biased version. Wide grip seated row for the same elbow flare with a fixed bar. Rope crossover seated row to exaggerate the spread.

Watch: Rushing the finish. The whole value is in the last few inches, so a pause at the squeeze is worth more here than extra weight.

remada_baixa_pegada_aberta.html:
Prescribed in ABCD01, ABCD08 and ABCD11. The wide pronated grip forces the elbows out away from the body, which trades lat involvement for upper-back and rear-delt work. When a program already has two lat-biased pulls, this is what fills the gap between the shoulder blades.

Hits: Rhomboids, mid traps and rear delts, with the lats reduced to a supporting role.

Purpose: Upper-back thickness from a rowing pattern, covering the plane that close-grip rows miss.

Swap with: Cable row with rope for more freedom at the finish. Reeves row for the free-weight version. Face pulls if you want the rear delt alone.

Watch: Shrugging. If the upper traps take over at the top, lower the weight and think about pulling the elbows back rather than the hands in.

remada_baixa_unilateral.html:
One arm on the cable row, prescribed in ABCD06. The cable's constant tension plus a unilateral arm path gives you the longest range of any seated rowing variation — the working arm can reach fully forward and pull fully back with a slight torso rotation at each end.

Hits: One lat through a long range, biceps assisting, obliques controlling the rotation.

Purpose: Fixing or preventing a side-to-side imbalance with the torso supported and the tension constant.

Swap with: One-arm DB row for the free weight version. Knee single arm low row for more range. Single arm pulldown if you want unilateral work vertically instead.

Watch: Letting the torso rotate so far that the movement becomes a twist. A little rotation extends the range; a lot replaces the lat with the obliques.

remada_com_kettlebell.html:
A bent-over row with kettlebells held overhand, prescribed once in ABCD03. The kettlebell's offset handle means the weight hangs below and behind the grip, which adds a rotational demand at the wrist and forearm that a dumbbell does not have.

Hits: Lats and mid traps, with more forearm work than an equivalent dumbbell row because of the offset load.

Purpose: Novelty and grip. In an intensification block it is a way to make a familiar pattern feel different without changing the pattern.

Swap with: One-arm DB row or bent over dumbbell row pronated — functionally the same movement with an easier implement.

Watch: The handle rotating in your hand under load. Grip it firmly and keep the wrist straight.

remada_baixa_pegada_inversa.html:
The close supinated seated row, prescribed in ABC03 as the fifth back movement of a pull day that already had twenty-three sets of back work. Turning the palms up tucks the elbows and drives the lats through a longer contraction than a neutral or pronated grip allows.

Hits: Lower lats with strong biceps involvement.

Purpose: A fifth back line that reaches the lower lat, in the most back-specialised block your trainer ever wrote.

Swap with: Wide underhand seated row is the version you actually run. V-bar pulldown for a similar elbow path vertically. Reverse grip triangle row.

Watch: Elbow strain from supinated pulling volume; if the inner elbow talks, move to a neutral handle.

lat_pullover.html:
Arms nearly straight, pulling a cable from overhead down to the thighs. Keeping the elbows locked takes the biceps out of the movement entirely, which makes it the only back exercise in this atlas where the lats work without the arms getting in the way. That is genuinely useful in a back session, because on every row and pulldown the biceps fail before the lats do.

Hits: Lats alone, through the shoulder-extension half of their range. The rear delt and the long head of the triceps assist by holding the arm straight.

Purpose: Lat isolation with the biceps removed. Used before rows it pre-exhausts the lats; used after, it finishes them once the arms have quit. In ABC+D2 it sat in the second half of pull day doing the latter.

Swap with: Straight arm pulldown with a bar, which is the same movement with fixed hands. Rope straight arm pulldown for more range at the bottom. Dumbbell pullover for the free-weight version with a stretch at the top.

Watch: Bending the elbows as it gets hard, which silently converts it into a pulldown. Fix the elbow angle and let the shoulder do all the moving.

pullover_pull_over_dumbell.html:
Lying across or along a bench, a single dumbbell lowered behind the head and pulled back over the chest. It is the one movement that genuinely sits between chest and back — the lats and the pecs both pull the arm from overhead toward the body, so both work, and which one does more depends on how bent your elbows are and how much you flare them. Bent and flared favours the chest; straighter and tucked favours the lats.

Hits: Lats through a deep overhead stretch, with the pec, serratus and long head of the triceps all contributing. It is also the best serratus movement in the atlas, which matters for overhead shoulder health.

Purpose: Ribcage and lat stretch under load, plus serratus work that nothing else covers. Old-school programs used it for exactly this and ABCD09 and ABCD11 brought it back.

Swap with: Cable lat pullover for constant tension and no stretch. Barbell pullover lying horizontal for more load. Decline pullover to increase the stretch further.

Watch: The overhead stretch at the bottom is a real shoulder position. Go light, and if the front of the shoulder pinches, shorten the range rather than pushing through it.

seated_lat_pull_in.html:
Seated with the cable in front, arms straight, pulling the handle in toward the hips in an arc. It opens ABCD09's pull day, which is an interesting choice: leading with a lat isolation movement pre-exhausts the lats before the T-bar row and the Reeves row, so the rows themselves become harder at lighter loads. That is a pre-exhaust strategy, and ABCD09 was tagged accumulation.

Hits: Lats through shoulder extension, rear delt assisting, biceps entirely absent.

Purpose: Pre-exhausting the lats so the rows that follow load the back rather than the arms, and warming the shoulder through a full range before anything heavy.

Swap with: Cable lat pullover standing or kneeling. Straight arm pulldown. Incline straight arm pulldown for the longest version.

Watch: Using the torso. Keep the chest up and still; only the arms travel.

levantamento_terra.html:
Prescribed exactly once in nineteen programs — ABC03, where it opened leg day with three warm-up sets of ten and then four working sets of ten. That single appearance is one of the most informative facts in the whole atlas. ABC03 was the specialization block that shifted leg day toward the posterior chain and cut quad work from seventeen sets to nine. The deadlift is what it shifted to.

Hits: Everything on the back of the body at once — erectors, glutes and hamstrings as the movers, lats and mid traps holding the bar against the body, forearms holding on. It is the broadest single movement here.

Purpose: Whole-posterior-chain loading in one lift. Nothing else in the atlas trains hip extension, spinal stabilisation and grip together under a load this heavy.

Swap with: Rack pulls for the top half with far less lower-back fatigue. Romanian deadlift if you want the hamstring stretch rather than the floor pull. Behind the back deadlift, which you have logged, for a quad-and-glute biased version with a shorter range.

Watch: This is the most technically demanding lift in the atlas and the one with the highest cost for getting it wrong. Set the back before the bar moves, keep the bar against the legs, and stop the set when the position changes — not when the reps run out.

rack_pulls.html:
A deadlift starting from pins set at or just below the knee, so you only do the top half. Removing the hardest part off the floor means you can load it heavier than a full deadlift, and the work lands on the upper back and erectors rather than the legs. Your two hundred and ten pounds here is the heaviest logged load of any back movement.

Hits: Erectors and mid traps as the primary, with the glutes finishing the lockout and the lats and forearms holding the bar. The hamstrings barely feature because the stretch never happens.

Purpose: Heavy upper-back and erector loading without the recovery cost of a full deadlift. In ABCD09's accumulation block it appeared on the upper day, which tells you it was being used as a back exercise rather than a leg one.

Swap with: Deadlift if you want the full range. Snatch-grip rack pull for more upper-back involvement. Barbell shrug if the goal is purely traps.

Watch: Heavy partials tempt you into rounding the upper back and hitching the lockout. Set the pin height so the bar starts just below the knee and keep the chest up.

viking_press_p_seated_p.html:
A landmine-style apparatus with fixed neutral handles that press up and slightly forward on an arc. The neutral grip and the arc are the point: both are easier on the shoulder than a straight barbell overhead press, which is why this carries a hundred and ninety-five pounds while your dumbbell pressing sits far lower. It appears in ABC+D1, ABC+D2 and ABC+D3 — all three of your own programs.

Hits: Front delt primarily, with the side delt, triceps and upper pec assisting. Seated removes the legs and the lower back entirely.

Purpose: Heavy overhead pressing in a shoulder-friendly path. It is the movement that lets an overhead press stay in the program when a straight bar would not be tolerated.

Swap with: Machine shoulder press for a similar fixed path. Half-kneeling landmine press if no Viking apparatus exists — it is the same arc one arm at a time. Neutral grip dumbbell press for the free-weight version.

Watch: Ribs flaring and the lower back arching to finish the press. Brace the trunk and stop the rep where the shoulders run out, not where the spine takes over.

klokov_press.pattern: vertical press, snatch grip behind neck
klokov_press.html:
A behind-the-neck press taken with a very wide snatch grip, named after the weightlifter Dmitry Klokov. The wide grip and the behind-neck path rotate the shoulder fully outward, which shifts the work from the front delt to the side and rear heads and demands a lot of shoulder mobility. Thirty-five pounds is the correct weight for it and your eleven logged sessions at that load show it was being used properly.

Hits: Side and rear delt, upper traps, with the front delt taking less than in any other press. It doubles as an external-rotation mobility drill under load.

Purpose: Pressing the heads of the deltoid that normal pressing misses, and maintaining overhead mobility. In ABCD10 it sat on pull day rather than push day, which is the correct read of what it trains.

Swap with: Behind the neck press with a normal grip if the snatch width is too much. Barbell Cuban press for a similar rotation emphasis. Face pulls if the overhead position is not available to you.

Watch: This movement requires real shoulder mobility and punishes its absence. If you cannot hold the bar behind your neck comfortably with no weight, do not load it. Keep it light forever — it is not a strength lift.

desenvolvimento_arnold.html:
Start with the palms facing you at chin height and rotate them outward as you press. The rotation is the whole difference from a standard dumbbell press: it takes the shoulder through internal-to-external rotation while under load, which brings the side delt in far more than a straight press does and gives the cuff work as a side effect.

Hits: Front and side delt together, with the triceps at lockout and genuine rotator cuff involvement through the turn.

Purpose: Covering two delt heads in one pressing movement. In a program short on slots it does the job of a press and a partial raise at once.

Swap with: DB shoulder press if you want pure pressing. Neutral-to-twisting dumbbell press is the same idea. Incline Cuban press for more rotation and less press.

Watch: Rotating too early or too late. The turn should happen through the middle third of the press, not at the bottom where the shoulder is most vulnerable.

desenvolvimento_maquina.html:
Seated, back supported, fixed handle path. It appears in three programs and is listed twice in the app under slightly different names, which is why the numbers look thin. Its value is the same as every machine in this atlas: the target muscle can be driven close to failure without the trunk or the balance giving out first.

Hits: Front delt with side delt and triceps assisting, and nothing else.

Purpose: Safe overhead pressing volume, usually after a free-weight press has already happened.

Swap with: Seated Viking press for a friendlier arc with more load. DB shoulder press for the free version. Hammer strength shoulder press for independent arms.

Watch: Seat height — handles should start at about shoulder level. Too low and you are pressing from a position that pinches.

desenvolvimento_com_halteres.html:
The default overhead press across ABC01, ABC05 and two ABCD blocks, always sitting after the chest work on push day. Independent dumbbells let each arm find its own path and allow the hands to converge at the top, which a barbell cannot do.

Hits: Front delt primarily, side delt and triceps assisting, upper pec contributing at the bottom.

Purpose: The shoulder press slot on a push day whose heavy work has already gone to the chest. It is deliberately not the hardest thing in the session.

Swap with: Seated Viking press, which is what you actually do. Arnold press for extra side-delt involvement. Machine shoulder press if the shoulder is tired.

Watch: Getting the dumbbells to the start position. Kick them up from the thighs one at a time rather than curling them into place.

lu_lateral_raise.html:
Named after the weightlifter Lu Xiaojun: a lateral raise that does not stop at shoulder height but continues all the way overhead until the plates or dumbbells nearly touch. Taking the arm past ninety degrees brings the upper traps in and keeps tension on the side delt through a range a normal raise abandons. Seventeen sessions at seventeen pounds is exactly the right way to run it.

Hits: Side delt through an unusually long range, upper traps through the top half, and the cuff working to keep the shoulder tracking as the arm goes overhead.

Purpose: Side-delt work plus overhead mobility in one movement. ABC+D1 ran it directly after the Viking press, so the shoulder got a full-range lightweight movement immediately after a heavy short-range one.

Swap with: Lateral raise if the overhead portion is uncomfortable. Around the worlds for a similar full-arc idea. Incline dumbbell Y raise for the overhead position with the torso supported.

Watch: The weight. This is a seventeen-pound movement, not a thirty-pound one, and the overhead half is where too much load turns into a shrug-and-heave.

elevacao_lateral_com_halteres.html:
Eleven programs prescribed it, making it the most-prescribed shoulder raise you have, and it is the reason the side delt stayed in the program at all — no press trains it properly. The reason your logged count is low is that in your own blocks you replaced it with the Lu and Jayme variants, both of which are better versions of the same idea.

Hits: Side delt alone if done well, upper traps if the weight is too heavy and you shrug.

Purpose: Shoulder width. It is the single most important non-pressing shoulder movement and the reason it appears in more than half your programs.

Swap with: Lu lateral raise for the longer range. Jayme or cable lateral raise for tension at the bottom. Thumbs-down lateral raise to bias the rear fibres, though it is harder on the joint.

Watch: Shrugging and swinging, which are the two ways this movement stops working. Lead with the elbow, stop at shoulder height, and pick a weight you can stop cleanly.

elevacao_unilateral.html:
One arm at a time, usually while holding something with the other for balance. Prescribed in five programs, generally as the second shoulder raise on pull day after the reverse fly. Doing one side at a time lets you hold the top position longer and lean slightly to extend the range.

Hits: Side delt, with the obliques on the opposite side bracing if you lean.

Purpose: A second lateral raise with a different quality — slower, longer, more controlled than the bilateral version.

Swap with: Jayme lateral raise, which is the cable version of this idea. Lateral raise bilateral for efficiency. Lying side lateral raise.

Watch: Using the lean to throw the weight up. Anchor firmly with the free hand.

elevacao_frontal_com_halteres.html:
Raising the arm straight forward to shoulder height. Six programs include it, usually bi-set with a press, and it is the most questionable-value movement in the shoulder section — the front delt is already trained by every press in the program. It earns its place only as a finisher or as part of a sequence.

Hits: Front delt, with the upper pec and upper traps contributing.

Purpose: Finishing the front delt after pressing, usually as the second half of a bi-set where the point is accumulated fatigue rather than new stimulus.

Swap with: Reeves front raise for a version with more of a grip and upper-back demand. Lateral raise if you would rather spend the slot on the head that is actually under-trained. Plate front raise for a neutral grip.

Watch: Swinging from the hips. Also worth asking honestly whether this slot would be better spent on a rear delt movement.

reeves_front_raise.html:
A front raise done gripping the plates of a barbell rather than the bar, the same Steve Reeves trick as the Reeves row. The extreme width means the shoulders have to work in a wider plane than a dumbbell allows and the grip becomes a genuine limiting factor. Ten pounds is the honest load for it.

Hits: Front delt across a wide plane, upper traps at the top, and real forearm and grip work from holding the plates.

Purpose: A front raise that is also grip work, in a block that was already running Reeves rows — a deliberate theme rather than a random pick.

Swap with: Front raise plain with dumbbells. Plate front raise holding a single plate at the edges. Lateral raise if the front delt does not need more work.

Watch: Dropping the bar. Grip fails suddenly on this one, so keep it light and stop the set with something left.

elevacao_lateral_e_frontal_com_halteres.pt: Elevação Lateral e Frontal com Halteres
elevacao_lateral_e_frontal_com_halteres.html:
Four sets of ten alternating between a lateral and a front raise without putting the dumbbells down — ABC01's way of covering two delt heads in one slot. It is a density technique as much as an exercise: the same total work in half the time, with the front raise serving as the “rest” for the side delt and vice versa.

Hits: Side and front delt in alternation, upper traps throughout.

Purpose: Two raises in one slot on a three-day program where slots are scarce. This is what an accumulation block does when it needs coverage without extra session length.

Swap with: Lateral raise alone if you only have one slot and want the under-trained head. Arnold press covers both heads in a single pressing movement. Any lateral plus any front raise as separate straight-set lines.

Watch: Fatigue turning both movements into swings by the third set. Use a weight chosen for the end of the sequence, not the start.

crucifixo_inverso.html:
Bent over or on an incline bench, arms nearly straight, opening out to the sides. Eight programs and ten logged sessions makes it the most consistently used rear-delt movement you have, and it is in the program for the reason described at the top of this section: no press trains the rear delt, so without a movement like this the head simply does not get worked. ABC+D1 ran the cable version for a better resistance curve.

Hits: Rear delt primarily, with the rhomboids and mid traps taking a share at the end of the range. Keeping the elbows nearly locked is what stops it becoming a row.

Purpose: The rear delt, and shoulder balance generally. A shoulder that presses a lot and never pulls backward drifts forward over years; this is the counterweight.

Swap with: Face pulls for more rotation and upper-back involvement. Cable reverse fly for constant tension. Reverse pec deck if you want a fixed path and easy failure work.

Watch: Bending the elbows to move more weight, which turns it into a wide row. This is a light movement done well; the thirty-two-pound top load is not a limitation.

facepull_halter.html:
Pulling toward the face with the elbows high and the hands finishing above the elbows, which combines a horizontal pull with an external rotation. That combination is why face pulls have a reputation as the single best shoulder-health movement: they train the rear delt, the mid back and the external rotators in one rep, all of which oppose the forward-rolled position that heavy pressing encourages.

Hits: Rear delt and rotator cuff as the primary targets, mid traps and rhomboids assisting. This is the rare movement where the prehab muscles are the main event rather than an afterthought.

Purpose: Undoing pressing. If you only add one movement to a program that presses heavily, this is the one with the best case.

Swap with: Cable face pulls with a rope, which is the standard and better version. Reverse fly if you want rear delt without the rotation. Band pull-aparts as a zero-equipment daily option.

Watch: Turning it into a row by dropping the elbows. Keep the upper arms at shoulder height and finish with the hands beside the ears.

smith_machine_upright_row.html:
Your most-logged shoulder movement outside the rotations — eighteen sessions, sixty-one working sets, all in ABCD11. Pulling the Smith bar straight up the body along its fixed track hits the side delt and upper traps together, and the fixed path means you do not have to manage the bar drifting away from you as it rises.

Hits: Side delt and upper traps as co-primaries, with the rear delt and biceps assisting. It is the one movement that loads the side delt heavily rather than in the raise's light range.

Purpose: Heavy side-delt and trap work. Raises cannot be loaded much; an upright row can, which is why a program that wants the side delt to actually grow includes one.

Swap with: EZ bar upright row for a wrist-friendlier grip. Behind-the-back upright row to reduce the internal rotation. Rope upright row for free hand position and less joint stress.

Watch: This is the movement in the shoulder section most likely to cause impingement, because pulling the hands up in front of the body internally rotates the shoulder at the same time. Keep the hands at least shoulder-width apart, stop the pull at chest height rather than chin height, and drop it entirely if the front of the shoulder pinches.

behind_the_back_upright_row.html:
The bar runs up behind your legs and back rather than in front. That single change fixes the main problem with upright rows: because the arms travel behind the body instead of in front of it, the shoulder is not internally rotated at the top, so the impingement risk largely disappears. ABCD09 used it as the upper-back and delt line on pull day.

Hits: Side delt and upper traps, with the rear delt taking more than a conventional upright row because the arms are behind the torso.

Purpose: Loadable side-delt work that the shoulder actually tolerates. If the conventional upright row bothers you, this is the version to keep.

Swap with: Behind the back upright row on a cable for constant tension. Smith machine upright row if you want more load and the shoulder is fine with it. Reeves deadlift for a related wide-grip behind-body pull.

Watch: The bar scraping up the backs of your legs. Stand a few inches forward of it and keep the path vertical.

remada_alta.html:
The conventional free-weight upright row, prescribed twice and in ABC02 combined with a front raise as a single line. It is the movement the Smith and behind-the-back versions are both variations on, and the one with the most shoulder risk of the three because nothing controls the bar path or the rotation.

Hits: Side delt and upper traps, biceps assisting.

Purpose: Loadable side delt work with a barbell — the cheapest way to get it when no machine is available.

Swap with: Behind-the-back upright row as the shoulder-friendly version. Smith machine upright row for the guided path. Lateral raise if the joint objects to the pattern at all.

Watch: Narrow grips and high pulls are the two things that make this movement hurt. Hands wider than shoulders, stop at chest height.

meadows_curl.html:
Your most-logged curl. Named after John Meadows, it uses a landmine or a low cable with the torso leaned forward so the working arm hangs behind the body line. That position keeps the biceps under stretch at the bottom and puts the hardest part of the rep in the first half, which is the opposite of a preacher curl and exactly why a program would run both.

Hits: Biceps at its longest length, with the brachialis underneath and the forearms holding on. The stretched position emphasises the long head.

Purpose: Loading the stretched end of the curl. ABCD10 paired it with a cable preacher curl so the two movements covered opposite ends of the strength curve in one session.

Swap with: Incline dumbbell curl is the closest match and needs only a bench. Bayesian cable curl standing with the cable behind you. Spider curl for the opposite end if that is what you want instead.

Watch: Letting the shoulder drift forward to help. The upper arm should stay behind the torso for the whole rep; if it swings forward, the stretch is gone and so is the point.

rosca_45.html:
Seated on a bench inclined to about forty-five degrees with the arms hanging straight down behind the torso line. It is the simplest way to get the stretched-biceps position and it appears in four programs including ABCD09, ABCD10 and ABCD11. The load is modest by design; there is no way to cheat a rep from this position.

Hits: Biceps long head especially, since that is the head that crosses the shoulder and therefore gets stretched when the arm goes behind the body. Brachialis assists.

Purpose: Stretch-position curling with nothing but a bench and dumbbells. It is the most accessible movement in this category.

Swap with: Meadows curl for the cable version with better tension at the bottom. Bayesian cable curl. Barbell dead stop cheat curl if you want to load the stretch heavier.

Watch: Shoulders rolling forward off the bench as you tire. Keep the back of the shoulder in contact with the pad.

rosca_direta_biceps_direto.html:
The default curl, logged under two Portuguese names across six programs. Both hands on one bar means the weight can be higher than any dumbbell version, and the fixed grip means the forearms cannot rotate — which is a limitation for the biceps' second function but an advantage for loading the first.

Hits: Both heads of the biceps evenly, brachialis and forearms assisting. Hardest through the middle of the range where the forearm is horizontal.

Purpose: The loadable curl and the reference arm movement. When a program wants one number to track for biceps progression, this is it.

Swap with: EZ bar curl if the straight bar bothers your wrists — it is the same movement with a kinder grip. Cable rope curl for constant tension. Dumbbell curls if you want the rotation back.

Watch: Swinging from the hips and letting the elbows drift forward at the top, both of which hand the work to the front delts. If the bar has to travel out and around, the weight is too heavy.

biceps_direto_sentado.html:
A barbell curl done seated, which removes the option of using the hips and legs to start the rep. That is the whole modification and it is a good one — the load drops from fifty pounds standing to thirty-five seated, and the difference is the cheating you were doing without noticing.

Hits: Biceps and brachialis, with no possible contribution from anywhere else.

Purpose: An honest curl. Useful as a check on what your standing number actually means, and as a strict finisher.

Swap with: Preacher curl for even more strictness. Barbell curl standing if you want the load. Cable preacher curl for constant tension and no cheating.

Watch: Leaning back against the bench to generate momentum, which is the seated version of swinging.

barbell_dead_stop_cheat_curl.html:
