The bar starts from a dead stop each rep, and a controlled amount of body english is allowed to get it moving. This is a deliberate rule break: the point is to use a load the biceps cannot lift strictly and then lower it slowly, so the negative does the work the positive could not. ABCD09 ran it in the arms slot.

Hits: Biceps and brachialis on the way down more than the way up, with the forearms and front delt involved in the cheat.

Purpose: Overload through the eccentric. It is the curl equivalent of a pin press — more load than the strict range allows, deliberately.

Swap with: Barbell curl strict if you would rather not use momentum. Cheat-and-slow-negative curl with dumbbells. Preacher curl with a drop set for a safer overload route.

Watch: The cheat becoming the whole rep. The body english should start the bar and nothing more, and the lowering should be slow and deliberate. Also watch the lower back, since the heave comes from there.

biceps_pulley_corda.html:
A rope on a low pulley, hands neutral, and in ABC01 and ABC+D1 it carries the four-rung descending-rep pyramid — twenty to thirty reps, then fifteen to twenty, then ten to fifteen, then five to ten. That structure is a small piece of programming cleverness: the high-rep rungs thoroughly warm the elbow before the heavy rung arrives, which matters for a joint that gets cranky.

Hits: Biceps and brachialis together because of the neutral grip, with the forearms taking real work from the rope. Constant cable tension means no rest point in the rep.

Purpose: Constant-tension curling and the natural home for high-rep pyramid work. It is the curl a program uses when it wants volume and joint safety rather than a maximum.

Swap with: Cable curl with a straight bar for more biceps and less brachialis. Alternating hammer curl for the same neutral grip with dumbbells. Cable preacher curl if you want the strict version.

Watch: Elbows travelling forward at the top. Keep them pinned to your sides and let the rope ends separate as the hands rise.

rosca_martelo_alternada.html:
Palms facing each other throughout, one arm at a time. The neutral grip takes the biceps out of its strongest position and hands more of the work to the brachialis, the muscle sitting underneath and slightly outside the biceps. Training it adds width to the upper arm in a way that supinated curling does not, which is why five of your programs include a hammer curl alongside a normal one.

Hits: Brachialis first, biceps second, with the brachioradialis in the forearm taking a real share. This is the most forearm-heavy curl in the section apart from the finger work.

Purpose: Brachialis and forearm thickness, and a grip position that is usually comfortable when a supinated curl has started to irritate the elbow.

Swap with: Cable rope curl for the same grip with constant tension. Bench hammer curl for a stricter version. Zottman curl if you want both grips in one movement.

Watch: Alternating turns it into a rest for each arm, so the tempo can drift. Keep it deliberate rather than swinging one up as the other comes down.

rosca_martelo_no_banco.html:
A hammer curl with the upper arm braced against an incline bench, so the shoulder cannot contribute at all. It is the strict version of the hammer curl, and the thirty-pound load against thirty-six standing is the measure of how much the standing version borrows from elsewhere.

Hits: Brachialis and biceps with the forearms assisting, and no shoulder involvement whatsoever.

Purpose: Strict neutral-grip curling, usually as a finisher once the heavier work is done.

Swap with: Alternating hammer curl standing. Cable rope curl. Preacher curl with a neutral grip if your bench allows it.

Watch: Little to go wrong. Keep the arm against the pad and resist shortening the range as it gets hard.

rosca_com_halteres.html:
Both arms, dumbbells, palms up. The advantage over a barbell is that the hands can rotate, so you can start neutral and supinate as you curl — which trains the biceps' second job of turning the palm upward rather than only its first job of bending the elbow.

Hits: Biceps including the supination function, brachialis and forearms assisting.

Purpose: The general-purpose curl in programs without a barbell slot for arms.

Swap with: Barbell curl for more load. Alternating DB curl for one arm at a time. Cable rope curl for constant tension.

Watch: Elbows drifting forward and the shoulders shrugging on the last reps.

rosca_alternada.html:
One arm at a time with a supinated grip. Alternating gives each arm a brief rest between reps, which means you can use slightly more weight per arm than curling both together, at the cost of a longer set.

Hits: Biceps with supination, brachialis and forearms assisting.

Purpose: Letting each arm work at its own level and fixing a side-to-side difference that a barbell would hide.

Swap with: Dumbbell curls both arms. Alternating hammer curl for the neutral grip. Concentration curl for a stricter unilateral option.

Watch: The resting arm's torso leaning to help the working arm.

biceps_pulley.html:
A straight or EZ bar on a low pulley. Same pattern as a barbell curl with the cable's constant tension replacing gravity's, which removes the easy spot at the top of the rep.

Hits: Biceps with brachialis assisting, loaded through the whole range rather than just the middle.

Purpose: Curling with no rest point, usually as the second arm movement.

Swap with: Cable rope curl, which is what you actually run. Barbell curl. Cable preacher curl for the strict version.

Watch: Standing too close to the pulley, which makes the bottom of the movement weightless.

rosca_scott_polia.html:
A preacher bench with a cable instead of free weight, which is the best possible version of this movement. The preacher position — upper arm angled forward against a pad — already makes the top of the curl hardest and eliminates cheating entirely; adding cable tension means the bottom is loaded too. ABCD10 and ABCD11 both ran it, the former as a four-rung pyramid.

Hits: Biceps short head especially, because the arm being in front of the body puts the long head in a shortened position where it can contribute less. Brachialis assists.

Purpose: Peak-contraction curling with no momentum available. Paired with the Meadows curl in ABCD10, it gave the session both ends of the strength curve.

Swap with: Preacher curl with a barbell or EZ bar. Preacher curl machine for a fixed path. Spider curl on the vertical side of an incline bench for a similar arm angle.

Watch: Extending fully at the bottom under cable tension puts a real stretch on the elbow tendon. Come almost straight rather than locking out hard, especially with weight on.

rosca_scott.html:
The free-weight version on a preacher bench, usually with an EZ bar. The pad under the upper arm is doing something specific: it stops the elbow travelling backward, which is the movement people unconsciously use to cheat a curl. Nothing else in the biceps section is this strict.

Hits: Biceps short head, brachialis and forearms assisting, hardest near the top.

Purpose: Strict curling, and a test of what your biceps can actually do without help. In three programs it sits as the second biceps movement after something looser.

Swap with: Cable preacher curl for tension at the bottom too. Preacher curl machine if the bar is awkward. Concentration curl for a similar strictness one arm at a time.

Watch: The bottom. Letting the arm snap straight under load on a preacher bench is the classic way to strain a biceps tendon. Stop just short of full extension.

rosca_scott_maquina.html:
Prescribed in five programs, which makes it the most-prescribed preacher variant, with a single logged session at seventy pounds — the heaviest curl load in the atlas, which is what a machine's fixed path and supported arms buy you. Its job is always the same: the last arm movement of the session, where going to failure matters more than technique.

Hits: Biceps short head with brachialis assisting, fully supported.

Purpose: Failure-safe biceps work at the end of a session. When a program wants a drop set on the arms, this is where it goes.

Swap with: Cable preacher curl for a similar feel with a better resistance curve. Preacher curl with an EZ bar. Concentration curl if no machine exists.

Watch: Seat and pad height, which change the movement completely. Set the armpits snug against the top of the pad.

arnold_concentration_curl.html:
The Arnold variant is done standing and bent over rather than seated with the elbow on the knee, so the arm hangs completely free and the dumbbell travels across the body toward the opposite shoulder. That crossing path is what distinguishes it: the biceps supinates and adducts at the same time, which reaches the fully shortened position better than a straight-up curl.

Hits: Biceps through its shortest position, with the brachialis assisting. The free-hanging arm means no pad is doing any of the work.

Purpose: Peak contraction one arm at a time, with a path that a bench-supported curl cannot reproduce. Ten sessions across two of your programs.

Swap with: Concentration curl seated for a more stable version. Cable preacher curl for constant tension at the top. Spider curl for the same shortened emphasis with both arms.

Watch: Swinging the torso to start the rep. The back stays still and only the forearm moves.

biceps_concentrado.html:
Eight programs prescribed it — the most of any biceps movement — and you have logged none, having substituted the Arnold variant instead. Seated, elbow braced against the inner thigh, curling straight up. The brace makes it the most stable curl available and the easiest place to feel the muscle actually working.

Hits: Biceps with brachialis assisting, elbow completely fixed.

Purpose: A strict finisher and the standard answer when a program wants one arm at a time. Its consistency across eight programs is the point: it is the low-risk default.

Swap with: Arnold concentration curl, which is what you run and is arguably better. Cable preacher curl. Preacher curl machine.

Watch: Using the leg to push the elbow upward as the set gets hard.

barbell_tricep_extension.html:
An overhead extension with a barbell or EZ bar, eleven logged sessions in ABCD09 and ABCD10. Using a bar rather than dumbbells means both arms share one load and the path is fixed, so you can go heavier than the single-arm versions while still getting the arm fully overhead. This is the workhorse long-head movement in your history.

Hits: Triceps long head at full stretch, lateral head assisting through the lockout. Overhead loading is what makes this different from everything in the pushdown group.

Purpose: Loading the biggest of the three triceps heads in the position where it is actually lengthened. In both programs it sits alongside a pushdown, covering the other two heads.

Swap with: DB French press for a similar overhead position with independent arms. Rope French press on a cable for constant tension. Kettlebell tricep extensions if the bar is uncomfortable overhead.

Watch: Elbows flaring out as the set gets hard, and the lower back arching to hold the bar up. Keep the elbows pointing forward and brace the trunk.

triceps_frances_halter.html:
A single heavy dumbbell held in both hands and lowered behind the head. The seventy-nine-pound load is the heaviest overhead triceps number in the atlas and it is achievable precisely because both hands share one weight and the path is short. The deep position behind the head is the whole reason to do it.

Hits: Triceps long head through the deepest stretch available in the section, lateral head at lockout.

Purpose: Heavy long-head loading. Where the barbell version is about a fixed path, this is about depth — a dumbbell can go further behind the head than a bar comfortably can.

Swap with: Barbell tricep extension for a fixed path. Rope French press for tension throughout. Single arm French press if the shoulder tolerates one side at a time better.

Watch: Elbow position at the bottom, where a heavy dumbbell wants to pull the shoulder into an extreme stretch. Control the descent and stop where the elbow, not the shoulder, is limiting.

triceps_frances_corda.html:
Facing away from a low or high pulley with a rope, pressing overhead and out. The cable keeps tension on the long head at the top of the rep where a dumbbell version goes almost weightless, and the rope lets the hands separate at lockout for a fuller contraction.

Hits: Triceps long head with constant tension, lateral head at the finish.

Purpose: Overhead triceps work with no rest point in the rep — the natural place for drop sets and rest-pause on the long head.

Swap with: DB French press for more load. Barbell tricep extension. Single arm cable overhead extension for unilateral work.

Watch: Drifting forward so the cable angle turns it into a pushdown. Keep the torso upright and the elbows high.

kettlebell_tricep_extensions.html:
Overhead extensions with a kettlebell, where the bell hangs below and behind the handle rather than in line with it. That offset changes the resistance through the rep and adds a wrist-stability demand that a dumbbell does not have — the bell wants to pull your hand backward at the bottom.

Hits: Triceps long head, with real forearm work from controlling the offset load.

Purpose: A different resistance profile on the long head, and a comfortable grip for people whose wrists object to a straight bar overhead.

Swap with: DB French press or barbell tricep extension for heavier loading. Rope French press for constant tension.

Watch: The bell rotating in your hand at the bottom. Grip the handle firmly and keep the wrist neutral.

triceps_frances_unilateral.html:
One dumbbell, one arm, overhead. Prescribed in four programs. Doing it one side at a time lets the free hand support the working elbow and lets each arm reach its own depth, which matters more here than on most movements because overhead range varies a lot between sides.

Hits: Triceps long head, one side at a time, with nothing else contributing.

Purpose: Long-head work with the range set by each arm individually, and a way to feel the muscle that bilateral versions can obscure.

Swap with: DB French press two-handed for load. Single arm cable overhead extension for constant tension. Rope French press.

Watch: The torso leaning away from the working arm. Stand or sit square.

triceps_frances.html:
The generic overhead extension, prescribed in three programs as the long-head half of the standard triceps pair. Whatever implement it used, its role in the session is always the same: the movement that does what a pushdown cannot.

Hits: Triceps long head at length, lateral head assisting.

Purpose: The overhead slot. It is the movement whose absence would leave two-thirds of the triceps under-trained.

Swap with: Barbell tricep extension or DB French press, both of which you actually run. Rope French press for tension throughout.

Watch: Elbow flare and lower-back arch, the two standard overhead-extension faults.

extensao_overhead_com_halteres.html:
Two dumbbells overhead, lowered behind the head independently. Prescribed once. Independent dumbbells mean each arm works through its own range, which is the advantage; the disadvantage is that the load per arm has to be modest.

Hits: Triceps long head, both arms independently.

Purpose: Overhead work with symmetry, in a program that wanted the long head trained without a bar.

Swap with: DB French press with one shared dumbbell for more load. Single arm French press. Rope French press.

Watch: Two dumbbells overhead is the least stable position in the triceps section. Sit with back support.

jm_press.html:
Named after powerlifter JM Blakley, this is deliberately halfway between a close-grip bench press and a skull crusher — the bar comes down toward the neck with the elbows tucked and travelling forward, so the triceps take a press-like load through an extension-like path. Your most-logged triceps movement, run in ABCD09 and ABCD10.

Hits: All three triceps heads, which is unusual — the hybrid path loads the long head more than a pushdown and the lateral and medial heads more than a pure overhead extension. Front delt and upper pec assist.

Purpose: Heavy triceps loading in a pressing pattern. It is the movement that lets a triceps session carry real weight without needing to be a bench press, which is why it earns a slot on both a push day and an upper day.

Swap with: Close grip bench press for more load and less triceps isolation. Skull crushers for a purer extension. Rolling DB tricep extension for a similar hybrid idea with dumbbells.

Watch: The elbow position, which is the whole movement. Elbows tucked and moving forward under the bar, not flared out. It should feel like the triceps are catching the bar, and it takes a few sessions to find. Start very light.

rolling_dumbbell_tricep_extension.html:
Lying down, the dumbbells lower past the head as in a skull crusher and then “roll” back — the shoulders extend so the weights travel further behind the head before the triceps press them back up. The rolling portion puts the long head into a deeper stretch than a fixed-elbow skull crusher reaches, and the press back out recruits everything.

Hits: Long and lateral heads together, with the front delt helping during the roll. It is the best stretch-plus-load combination in the triceps section.

Purpose: Getting a deep long-head stretch while still being able to press a real weight, because the roll lets the shoulder help through the hardest part.

Swap with: Skull crushers for the fixed elbow version. DB French press for the overhead stretch without the roll. JM press for a similar hybrid with a bar.

Watch: Rolling too far, which turns it into a pullover. The weights should travel behind the head, not down to the floor, and the elbows should stay roughly shoulder-width.

triceps_testa.html:
Ten programs prescribed it, making it the joint-most-prescribed triceps movement, and you have one logged session — having replaced it consistently with the JM press and the rolling extension, both of which are arguably better versions of the same idea. Lying down, elbows fixed, the bar lowers to the forehead and presses back.

Hits: Long head with the lateral head assisting, loaded with the arm roughly vertical so the long head is partly stretched.

Purpose: The standard lying triceps extension. Across ten programs it is the reliable default — simple to set up, easy to load, hard to get badly wrong.

Swap with: JM press for a heavier hybrid. Rolling DB extension for a deeper stretch. Incline DB skull crushers to increase the long-head stretch with an angle.

Watch: Elbows flaring outward, which hands the work to the chest, and the elbow joint complaining — this movement is the most common cause of triceps tendon irritation. Use an EZ bar and keep it moderate.

triceps_testa_halteres.html:
The dumbbell version, prescribed in five programs. Independent weights let each hand take a neutral grip, which most people find easier on the elbow than a straight bar, and let the dumbbells travel to either side of the head rather than stopping at the forehead.

Hits: Long head with the lateral head assisting, one arm's range unaffected by the other.

Purpose: Lying triceps extension for elbows that object to a bar. It is the accessible default.

Swap with: Rolling DB tricep extension, which is this movement with a better stretch. Skull crushers with an EZ bar. JM press.

Watch: Dropping a dumbbell on your face. Lower under control, and set up by pressing them to lockout first rather than starting from behind the head.

triceps_testa_inclinado_p_60_p.html:
A skull crusher on a bench set to sixty degrees, which is the most precise triceps prescription in your whole history. The angle matters: tilting the torso back moves the arm further overhead relative to the body, which puts the long head under more stretch than a flat skull crusher without needing a full overhead position.

Hits: Long head, more so than the flat version, lateral head assisting.

Purpose: A middle point between a skull crusher and a French press — more long-head stretch than the first, more stability than the second.

Swap with: Rolling DB tricep extension for a similar effect flat. DB French press for full overhead. Skull crushers flat if the bench is taken.

Watch: Shoulders rolling forward off the bench as the weights go behind the head.

triceps_corda.html:
Ten programs, and in ABC01, ABC02 and ABC+D1 it carries the same four-rung descending pyramid as the rope curl — twenty to thirty, fifteen to twenty, ten to fifteen, five to ten. That structure is the most sophisticated single touch in the early programs: the high-rep rungs warm the elbow thoroughly before the heavy rung, on a joint that does not tolerate going straight to heavy.

Hits: Lateral and medial heads, with the long head contributing little because the elbow is at the side and the long head is already slack. The rope lets the hands turn out at the bottom for a fuller contraction.

Purpose: The pushdown half of the standard triceps pair, and the safest place in an arm session to do very high reps.

Swap with: Triceps bar pushdown for more load and less hand freedom. Two D handle pushdown. Pushdown facing away if you want a different angle.

Watch: Leaning over the rope and turning it into a press. Stand upright with the elbows pinned and only the forearms moving.

triceps_pulley_p_facing_away_p.html:
Standing with your back to the stack so the cable runs over the shoulder and you extend forward and down. Turning around changes which head is emphasised: the arm ends up slightly in front of the body rather than beside it, which puts the long head under more tension than a conventional pushdown does.

Hits: Long head more than a normal pushdown, with the lateral head assisting.

Purpose: Getting some long-head stretch out of a pushdown pattern — useful when the shoulder will not tolerate a true overhead position.

Swap with: Rope French press for the full overhead version. Triceps rope pushdown conventional. Bayesian cable extension.

Watch: The cable rubbing the shoulder and the torso leaning forward for leverage. Set the pulley height so the rope clears cleanly.

two_d_handle_tricep_pushdown_p_overhand_.pt: Two D Handle Tricep Pushdown (Overhand Ending)
two_d_handle_tricep_pushdown_p_overhand_.html:
Two separate D handles instead of a rope or bar, finishing with the hands pronated. Independent handles let each arm travel its own path and the overhand finish rotates the forearm at the bottom, which adds a small amount of extra shortening at the end of the rep.

Hits: Lateral and medial heads, with the forearms involved in the rotation.

Purpose: A pushdown with independent arms and a rotational finish — mostly a detail variation on the rope version.

Swap with: Triceps rope pushdown, which does nearly the same thing. Single arm cable pushdown. Triceps bar pushdown.

Watch: Nothing unusual — keep the elbows pinned and do not lean.

triceps_kickback.html:
Bent over or standing, upper arm held parallel to the torso and behind the body, extending the forearm back. In ABC01 it was prescribed to failure at four sets of ten to fifteen. The arm being behind the body means the triceps reaches full shortening at the top, which no pushdown achieves — a pushdown runs out of range while the arm is still beside you.

Hits: Lateral head mainly, at full contraction, with the rear delt working to hold the upper arm in place.

Purpose: Peak contraction for the triceps. It is the shortest-range, lightest movement in the section and that is the point — it finishes the muscle rather than loading it.

Swap with: Barbell kickback for a two-handed version that is easier to keep strict. Cable kickback for constant tension. Triceps rope pushdown with a hard squeeze at the bottom.

Watch: The upper arm dropping as you tire, which shortens the range to nothing. If the shoulder cannot hold the arm up, the weight is too heavy.

tricep_barbell_kickback.html:
A kickback with both hands on a barbell behind the body, which fixes the hand position and makes it much easier to keep the upper arms still than the dumbbell version. ABCD09 also ran a standing head-height variant. Loading both arms on one bar means you can be slightly heavier while staying strict.

Hits: Lateral head at full contraction, rear delt holding position.

Purpose: A strict kickback. The bar removes the main fault of the dumbbell version, which is the arms drifting independently.

Swap with: Triceps kickback with dumbbells. Cable kickback. Bench dips if you want a loaded compound instead.

Watch: Rounding the back to hold the bent-over position for a long set. Brace or use a supported version.

bench_dips.html:
Hands on a bench behind you, feet out in front, lowering and pressing back up. Prescribed once. It is the zero-equipment triceps compound and it can be taken to failure without any risk of dropping anything, which is its main virtue.

Hits: Triceps primarily, with the front delt and lower pec assisting.

Purpose: Bodyweight triceps volume, usually at the end of a session.

Swap with: Dips on parallel bars for a better version. Triceps rope pushdown to failure. JM press if you want the loaded compound.

Watch: The shoulder. Hands behind the body with bodyweight on them puts the front of the shoulder in a stressed position, and going deep makes it worse. Keep the range modest, or choose parallel-bar dips instead.

smith_finger_curl.html:
Standing in the Smith machine holding the bar behind or in front of the thighs, letting it roll out to the fingertips and then closing the hand to curl it back. The Smith's fixed track is what makes this safe at a hundred and thirteen pounds — if your fingers open, the bar goes down the rails rather than onto your feet. It closes pull day in ABC+D1 and ABC+D2 at six sets of fifteen.

Hits: The deep finger flexors in the forearm, with the wrist flexors assisting. Nothing else in the atlas trains the hand this directly.

Purpose: Grip endurance, so that the hands are not what ends a set of heavy rows or deadlifts. Six sets of fifteen at the end of pull day is a high-volume, low-risk way to get it.

Swap with: Cable finger curl, which you also run and which is gentler on the wrist. Barbell finger curl behind the back if no Smith is free. Dead hangs for a static alternative.

Watch: Letting the bar roll all the way out of the hand. Control the opening as much as the closing — the eccentric is where the training effect is.

cable_finger_curl.html:
The same movement on a cable, which keeps tension constant through the roll-out and the close. Because the cable pulls at an angle rather than straight down, the wrist sits in a slightly easier position than the Smith version, which is why it is the one to use if the wrist complains.

Hits: Finger flexors with the wrist flexors assisting, loaded evenly throughout.

Purpose: Grip work with no rest point in the rep, and a wrist-friendly alternative to the Smith version.

Swap with: Smith finger curl for more load. Lying DB wrist curl if you want the wrist rather than the fingers. Finger plate grip with dip belt for a static hold.

Watch: Standing too close to the stack, which removes the load at the bottom of the roll.

t_bar_forearm_curl.html:
Using a landmine so the resistance arcs rather than pulling straight down, which changes the resistance profile across the wrist's range. The landmine's pivot means the load is lightest at the start and heaviest where the wrist is most flexed, roughly matching where the forearm is strongest.

Hits: Forearm flexors through wrist flexion, with the finger flexors assisting on the grip.

Purpose: Forearm size rather than grip endurance — this is the one movement in the section that is a wrist curl rather than a finger curl.

Swap with: Lying DB wrist curl for the conventional version. Barbell wrist curl over a bench. Cable finger curl if grip is the actual goal.

Watch: The wrist is a small joint and does not need much load. Keep the reps high and the weight modest.

lying_chest_supported_dumbbell_wrist_cur.en: Lying Chest Supported DB Wrist Curl
lying_chest_supported_dumbbell_wrist_cur.pt: Lying Chest Supported Dumbbell Wrist Curl
lying_chest_supported_dumbbell_wrist_cur.html:
Lying chest-down on a bench with the forearms hanging over the end, curling the dumbbells with the wrists alone. The chest support fixes the forearms completely, so nothing but the wrist can move — it is the strictest wrist curl available.

Hits: Forearm flexors in isolation, finger flexors on the grip.

Purpose: Strict forearm work. Prescribed in ABCD09 and ABCD10 as the last line of the day.

Swap with: T-bar forearm curl. Barbell wrist curl seated with the forearms on the thighs. Smith finger curl if grip endurance matters more.

Watch: Very little — it is about as safe as a movement gets. Keep the reps high.

finger_plate_grip_with_dipbelt.en: Finger Plate Grip with Dip Belt
finger_plate_grip_with_dipbelt.html:
Pinching plates between the fingers with extra load hanging from a dip belt. This is a pinch-grip hold, which trains the thumb and finger flexors isometrically rather than through a range — a genuinely different quality from the finger curls, and the hardest kind of grip to develop.

Hits: Finger and thumb flexors isometrically, with the forearm flexors and the traps holding everything in place.

Purpose: Pinch grip, which nothing else in the atlas trains. Useful mostly as a specific weak-point fix.

Swap with: Plate pinch holds without the belt. Farmer's walk for a crushing-grip alternative. Dead hangs. Smith finger curl if dynamic grip is the goal.

Watch: Dropping plates on your feet. Do it over a mat and stop the hold with something left.

agachamento_hack.html:
Nine programs and fifteen logged sessions, opening leg day in ABC01 with two warm-up sets. The machine holds your back against a pad at a fixed angle, which means your torso cannot lean forward to help — so the knees travel forward and the quads do the work that a free squat would share with the hips and lower back. This is your heaviest logged squat pattern at two hundred and forty-five pounds.

Hits: Quadriceps as the clear primary, with the glutes and adductors assisting at depth. The back pad removes the erectors entirely, which is the point.

Purpose: Heavy quad loading with no spinal cost. When a program wants leg day to start with something heavy but the block is already spending recovery on deadlifts or rows, the hack squat is the answer.

Swap with: Smith machine squat for a similar fixed-torso feel. Barbell hack squat for the free-weight version behind the legs. Leg press if the knees prefer less forward travel.

Watch: Foot placement, which changes everything — feet low on the platform means more knee travel and more quad, feet high means more hip and more glute. Pick one and stay with it across the block. Do not let the knees cave inward at the bottom.

witches_squat.html:
A squat performed on the toes with the heels raised and the torso held upright, so the knees travel very far forward and the hips barely move at all. It is close to a loaded sissy squat and it appears in all three of your own ABC+D blocks, run with drop sets in ABC+D1. The hundred-and-twelve-pound load reflects how hard the position is rather than any weakness.

Hits: Quadriceps through their shortest, most knee-dominant range, with the calves working hard to hold the raised heel position and the adductors assisting.

Purpose: Maximum quad isolation from a squat pattern, particularly the part of the quad closest to the knee. It is what you reach for when a leg day already has a heavy hip-involved squat.

Swap with: Crouched wall sissy squat or Zercher sissy squat for related positions. Leg extension for pure knee extension with no balance demand. Hack squat with feet low as the machine-supported version.

Watch: The knees. Extreme forward knee travel under load is exactly the position that aggravates a patellar tendon, so build into it gradually and stop if the front of the knee hurts rather than the muscle.

agachamento_smith.html:
Squatting with the bar on a fixed vertical track, which lets you stand with your feet further forward than a free squat would allow. That forward foot position plus the fixed bar path means the torso stays upright and the quads take the majority of the work — effectively a free-weight hack squat.

Hits: Quadriceps primarily, glutes and adductors assisting, with the erectors much less involved than a back squat.

Purpose: A quad-biased squat when the hack squat is taken. In ABCD09 it sat second on leg day behind the barbell hack squat.

Swap with: Hack squat for the machine version. Barbell hack squat. Leg press if you want to remove balance entirely.

Watch: The fixed track means your body has to accept the bar's path rather than the reverse, and standing too far forward puts a shear load on the knee. Find the foot position where the descent feels vertical and mark it.

barbell_hack_squat.html:
The original hack squat: a barbell held behind the legs, lifted from the floor in a squat. Because the bar is behind you the torso stays upright and the knees travel forward, giving a quad emphasis, and because you are holding the bar in your hands the grip and traps become a limiting factor. It opened ABCD09's leg day.

Hits: Quadriceps primarily, glutes at the top, with real forearm and trap work from holding the bar.

Purpose: A free-weight quad squat that needs no machine at all. In an accumulation block built on novelty, it is a squat pattern most people have never done.

Swap with: Hack squat machine for the same emphasis with no grip limit. Smith machine squat. Trap bar squat for a similar upright-torso feel with better handles.

Watch: The bar hitting the backs of your calves and heels on the way down. Also the grip failing before the legs do — straps solve it.

crouched_wall_sissy_squat.html:
A sissy squat braced against a wall, which solves the balance problem that makes unassisted sissy squats so awkward. The hips stay extended while the knees bend fully, which stretches the quad across both the hip and the knee at once — a position no other squat variation reaches. Thirty-two pounds is a serious load in this position.

Hits: Quadriceps, and specifically the rectus femoris, the one quad muscle that crosses the hip and therefore only gets fully loaded when the hip is extended. Adductors assist.

Purpose: Training the part of the quad that squats and leg presses under-train. It is the most anatomically specific movement in the quad section.

Swap with: Witches squat for a similar knee-dominant position. Zercher sissy squat. Reverse Nordic curl as the bodyweight progression. Leg extension if the knee will not tolerate it.

Watch: Knee tolerance. This is the highest patellar-load position in the atlas. Start unloaded, add weight only when the movement is comfortable, and never push through front-of-knee pain.

zercher_sissy_squat_zercher_sissy_squat_.pt: Zercher Sissy Squat · Zercher Sissy Squat Smith
zercher_sissy_squat_zercher_sissy_squat_.html:
A sissy squat with the load held in the crooks of the elbows. Holding the weight in front at chest height counterbalances the backward lean that makes a sissy squat hard to balance, so the movement becomes possible without a wall. The five-pound load in the Smith version tells you the position, not the weight, is the difficulty.

Hits: Quadriceps with the hip extended, adductors assisting, plus isometric work from the erectors and biceps holding the Zercher position.

Purpose: Sissy squatting without a wall, and a front-loaded position that keeps the torso upright by necessity rather than by discipline.

Swap with: Crouched wall sissy squat for more load. Witches squat. Goblet sissy squat holding a dumbbell at the chest, which is easier on the elbows.

Watch: The Zercher hold is uncomfortable on the elbow crease — use a pad or a towel. And as with all sissy work, the knees set the limit.

back_squat.html:
Prescribed in four programs, always second on leg day behind the hack squat, and in ABC01 it carried an ascending pyramid with ninety seconds rest — more rest than anything else in that session. Putting the free squat second rather than first is an interesting choice: the hack squat warms the knees and pre-fatigues the quads, so the back squat is performed at a lower absolute load but with better position.

Hits: The widest recruitment in the quad section — quads and glutes as co-primaries, with the adductors, erectors and hamstrings all contributing. The bar on the back is what brings the spine in.

Purpose: The reference leg lift and the one that loads the whole lower body as a system rather than a muscle.

Swap with: Smith machine squat or hack squat if the spinal load is the problem — both keep the quad stimulus and lose the systemic one. Front squat for a more upright torso. Leg press as the low-skill substitute.

Watch: Depth and knee tracking under fatigue. Set the depth you can reach with a neutral spine and treat losing it as the end of the set rather than something to grind through.

agachamento_bulgaro_p_com_halteres_p.html:
Rear foot elevated on a bench, front leg doing the squatting. Prescribed in ABC03 and two other blocks — notably in ABC03, the specialization block that shifted leg day toward the posterior chain, where a single-leg movement helps cover the hip without needing another loaded bilateral lift.

Hits: Quad and glute of the front leg together, with the split depending on torso lean — upright is more quad, leaned forward is more glute. Adductors and hamstrings stabilise.

Purpose: Heavy unilateral leg work with a long range, and the best single-leg strength builder available. It also exposes hip stability problems that bilateral squats hide.

Swap with: Dumbbell lunges, which you actually run and which cover a similar pattern with more movement. Smith machine lunge for a guided version. Single leg extension if balance is the obstacle.

Watch: Bench height and stride length, both of which change the movement completely. Too high a bench forces the hip into extension it does not have.

quad_focused_leg_press.html:
A leg press with the feet placed low and close on the platform, which increases how far the knees travel forward and cuts the hips out of the movement. Twenty logged sessions across ABCD09, ABCD10, ABCD11 and ABC+D1 makes this your single most-used leg movement, and ABCD10 ran it as the leading pyramid on leg day.

Hits: Quadriceps as the clear primary, with the adductors assisting at depth and the glutes contributing much less than a standard leg press. Zero spinal load.

Purpose: High-volume quad work with no recovery cost anywhere else. It is the movement that lets leg day carry real volume in a block whose heavy work is going elsewhere.

Swap with: Hack squat for a similar emphasis with a squat pattern. Leg press with a normal foot position if you want the glutes back in. Leg extension for pure knee extension.

Watch: The lower back rounding off the pad at the bottom, which is what happens when you chase depth the hips cannot give. Stop where the pelvis stays flat. Also do not lock the knees hard at the top.

leg_45_leg_press_45.html:
The most-prescribed leg movement in your history at thirteen of nineteen programs, and the most-used exercise across all sixteen of your trainer's programs. It sits third on leg day almost every time — after the squats, before the extensions — which is exactly where a movement belongs whose job is volume rather than intensity.

Hits: Quads and glutes together, with the split set by foot placement: feet high and wide is glute and adductor, feet low and narrow is quad. Hamstrings assist at depth.

Purpose: Safe, high-volume leg loading. The back support means you can accumulate sets after squatting without the spine or the nervous system being the limit.

Swap with: Quad focused leg press is the same machine with a specific foot position, and is what you run. Hack squat for a squat pattern with similar support. Leg extension plus hip thrust to split the two jobs apart.

Watch: Going so deep that the pelvis tucks under and the lower back lifts off the pad. Also the habit of loading the machine far past what the range can support — a partial-range leg press with six plates trains less than a full-range one with three.

cadeira_extensora.html:
Thirteen programs, tied with the leg press as the most-prescribed leg movement, and almost always carrying a technique — a drop set in ABC01, a bi-set with lunges in ABC02. Your two hundred and ninety-five pound top load is the heaviest number in the entire atlas, which says more about machine leverage than about strength.

Hits: Quadriceps and nothing else. It is the only true isolation movement for the quad, which is precisely its value and its limitation.

Purpose: Finishing the quads after the compounds, and the safest possible home for drop sets and failure work on legs. When a program wants the quads taken to genuine failure, it does it here.

Swap with: Single leg extension for unilateral work. Sissy squat variants for knee extension with the hip extended, which reaches the rectus femoris better. Quad focused leg press if the machine is taken.

Watch: Slamming into full lockout with a heavy stack, which puts a large shear force through the knee. Control the top, and set the seat so the knee joint lines up with the machine's pivot.

leg_extension_p_quase_leaning_back_p.html:
A leg extension with the torso reclined rather than upright. Leaning back opens the hip angle, which lengthens the rectus femoris — the one quad muscle that crosses the hip — and therefore loads it at a longer length than the standard seated position. The load drops from two hundred and ninety-five to a hundred and seventy, which is the measure of how much harder the position is.

Hits: Quadriceps with a specific emphasis on the rectus femoris, which upright extensions and leg presses both under-train.

Purpose: The same anatomical target as a sissy squat, reached from a machine with no balance or knee-position risk. A genuinely clever substitution.

Swap with: Crouched wall sissy squat for the free-weight equivalent. Reverse Nordic curl. Leg extension upright if the machine will not recline.

Watch: Sliding forward out of the seat as the load rises. Hold the handles and keep the hips pinned.

cadeira_extensora_unilateral.html:
One leg at a time on the extension machine, prescribed once. Doing it unilaterally lets each quad work to its own failure point and makes a side-to-side difference immediately obvious, which the bilateral version averages away.

Hits: One quadriceps in isolation.

Purpose: Correcting or checking an imbalance, and squeezing more quality work out of a single machine slot.

Swap with: Leg extension bilateral. Bulgarian split squat for a unilateral compound. Single leg press.

Watch: The hips twisting toward the working side. Sit square and hold the handles.

passada_com_halteres_afundo_com_halteres.pt: Passada com Halteres · Afundo com Halteres
passada_com_halteres_afundo_com_halteres.html:
Eight programs and fifteen logged sessions, almost always prescribed as three sets of twenty — a rep count that appears nowhere else in the atlas. Twenty reps per leg with dumbbells is not a strength prescription; it is a conditioning and hip-stability one, and it usually sits near the end of leg day where that makes sense. In ABC02 it was bi-set with the leg extension.

Hits: Quads and glutes of the front leg, with the adductors working hard on the step and the hamstrings stabilising. Longer steps shift it toward the glutes, shorter steps toward the quads.

Purpose: Unilateral work, hip stability, and the high-rep finisher role. It is also the only leg movement in most programs that involves actually moving through space.

Swap with: Smith machine lunge for a guided version with more load. Bulgarian split squat for a heavier, more strength-focused unilateral option. Reverse lunge if the knee prefers stepping back to stepping forward.

Watch: Form collapsing somewhere around rep twelve of twenty. The torso should stay upright and the front knee should track over the foot; when it stops doing either, the set is over.

avanco_smith.html:
A split-stance lunge with the bar on a fixed track, so the balance problem disappears and the load can go up considerably — eighty pounds against fifteen-pound dumbbells. The track means the movement is really a split squat rather than a walking lunge, since you stay in one place.

Hits: Quads and glutes of the front leg, adductors assisting, with no demand on balance at all.

Purpose: Loaded unilateral leg work. It is the bridge between a dumbbell lunge, which cannot be loaded much, and a Bulgarian split squat, which needs more stability.

Swap with: Bulgarian split squat for a longer range. Dumbbell lunges for the free version. Barbell split squat in a rack.

Watch: The fixed bar path dictating your stance. Set the front foot where the descent feels vertical, and keep the front heel down.

alongamentos.html:
Prescribed as the opening line of leg day in ABC03 and one other block. Worth noting because it is the only pure mobility line in any of the nineteen programs, and it appears in ABC03 — the block that introduced deadlifts and shifted the whole day toward the hips. A hip hinge needs range the hip does not automatically have, and the prescription reflects that.

Hits: Hip flexors, hamstrings and quads — range rather than load.

Purpose: Getting the hip ready for hinging. In a block introducing deadlifts to a body that had done nine weeks of machine squats, this was the sensible first line.

Swap with: Dynamic hip mobility work — leg swings, ninety-nineties, deep squat holds — all of which prepare the joint better than static stretching before lifting.

Watch: Long static holds immediately before heavy lifting can reduce force output temporarily. Save the long holds for after the session and do dynamic work before it.

cadeira_flexora.html:
Ten programs, and the one that carries the most interesting technique work in the whole atlas: ABC03 ran a truncated pyramid on it — two sets of twelve to fifteen, two of eight to twelve, two of five to eight — six quality sets with a built-in warm-up and a built-in heavy finish, on the day the block shifted toward the posterior chain. Seated rather than lying matters: with the hip flexed, the hamstring starts longer, which is where it responds best.

Hits: Hamstrings through knee flexion, at a longer muscle length than the lying version because of the hip angle. The calf assists, since the gastrocnemius also crosses the knee.

Purpose: The hamstring's knee function, loaded at length. It is the higher-value of the two curl variations for that reason.

Swap with: Lying leg curl if the seated machine is taken, accepting the shorter starting length. Nordic curl for a bodyweight version with a huge eccentric. Single leg seated curl for unilateral work.

Watch: The hips lifting off the seat to help, which shortens the range. Strap down if the machine has a lap pad, and control the return rather than letting the stack pull you back.

mesa_flexora.html:
Face down, curling the heels toward the glutes. With the hip neutral rather than flexed, the hamstring starts shorter than on the seated machine, so the hardest part of the rep moves toward the top. ABC02 gave it a drop set, which is exactly the right technique for a movement whose strength curve favours the finish.

Hits: Hamstrings through knee flexion with the calves assisting, and the glutes contributing slightly as the hips try to lift.

Purpose: The second curl variation, covering a different part of the hamstring's strength curve from the seated version. Several programs run both.

Swap with: Seated leg curl for more length. Nordic curl. Single leg lying curl.

Watch: The hips rising off the pad, which is the standard cheat here and turns the movement into a partial. Keep the pelvis pressed down.

wrapped_barbell_romanian_deadlift.html:
A Romanian deadlift — knees nearly straight, hips pushing back, bar tracing the legs down to mid-shin and back — with the bar wrapped, presumably for comfort against the legs. Twelve logged sessions across ABCD10 and ABCD11 makes it your primary hinge, which matters because this is the pattern the full deadlift was prescribed for exactly once and never logged.

Hits: Hamstrings under a long stretch and glutes at the top, with the erectors working isometrically and the lats holding the bar against the body. The stretch at the bottom is the whole point.

Purpose: The hamstring's hip function, which no leg curl trains. In a program whose leg day is otherwise quad-dominated, this is the movement that keeps the back of the leg in the plan.

Swap with: Stiff-leg deadlift, which is nearly the same movement. Good morning if you prefer the bar on your back. Single leg Smith good morning for a unilateral version. Seated leg curl only if you accept losing the hip function entirely.

Watch: Rounding the lower back to reach further down. The depth should be set by your hamstring flexibility, not by touching the floor — go down until the stretch arrives and the back is still flat, then come up.

stiff.html:
Prescribed in four programs as the hinge on leg day. Functionally almost identical to the Romanian deadlift — the distinction people draw is that a stiff-leg keeps the knees straighter and often starts from the floor, while an RDL starts from the top with a slight knee bend. Either way, the job is hip extension against a long hamstring.

Hits: Hamstrings at length, glutes at the top, erectors bracing throughout.

Purpose: The hinge slot. Four programs is enough to show your trainer considered it standard equipment for a complete leg day.

Swap with: Wrapped barbell RDL, which is what you actually run. Good morning. Behind the back deadlift for a different bar position.

Watch: Straighter knees mean a longer lever on the lower back, so this is more demanding on the spine than an RDL with soft knees. Keep the load moderate and the back flat.

good_morning.html:
The bar sits on your back as in a squat, and you hinge forward at the hips with the knees soft. Putting the load on the shoulders rather than in the hands makes the lever on the spine much longer than an RDL, which is why sixty pounds here is genuinely hard and why the erectors become almost a co-primary rather than a supporting player.

Hits: Hamstrings through hip flexion and the erectors holding the spine against a long lever, with the glutes finishing the movement.

Purpose: Training the hinge with a maximal demand on spinal bracing. It is the most direct erector-strengthening movement in the atlas after the deadlift.

Swap with: Wrapped barbell RDL for the same hamstring work with far less spinal load. Single leg Smith good morning, which you also run. Back extension if the bar on the back is the problem.

Watch: This has the worst consequences for bad form of any hamstring movement here. Keep the load light, brace hard, and stop at the depth where the back is still flat. Do not do this fatigued.

good_morning_smith_single_leg.html:
A good morning on one leg with the Smith bar providing both the load and the stability. The fixed track solves the balance problem that makes single-leg hinging awkward, so you can actually load it — seventy pounds on one leg against sixty on two for the barbell version. It ran in ABC+D1 and ABCD09.

Hits: One hamstring and glute through hip extension, with the erectors resisting rotation as well as flexion, and the adductors stabilising the standing hip.

Purpose: Unilateral hinging, which exposes and corrects a side-to-side difference that a barbell hinge averages out. The anti-rotation demand is a bonus nothing else in the section provides.

Swap with: Single leg RDL with a dumbbell for the free version. Good morning bilateral. Wrapped barbell RDL.

Watch: The hips rotating open toward the free leg. Keep them square to the floor, which is most of the difficulty.

behind_the_back_deadlift.html:
A deadlift with the bar behind the legs rather than in front. Moving the bar behind the body's centre line forces a much more upright torso, which shifts work from the lower back toward the glutes and quads and shortens the range considerably. It is closer to a barbell hack squat than to a conventional deadlift.

Hits: Glutes and quads as the movers, hamstrings assisting, with the traps and forearms holding the bar behind you — a genuinely awkward grip position.

Purpose: A hip-hinge pattern that does not load the lower back the way a conventional deadlift does. In a block already running RDLs and good mornings, this covers hip extension without stacking more spinal fatigue.

Swap with: Barbell hack squat, which is mechanically very similar. Glute hip thrust for glute work with no spinal load at all. Trap bar deadlift for a more upright conventional pull.

Watch: The bar catching on the backs of the legs and the shoulders rolling forward to hold it. Stand a little in front of the bar and keep the chest up.

deficit_behind_the_back_deadlift.html:
The behind-the-back deadlift performed standing on a three-plate deficit, which restores the range the behind-the-back bar position takes away. The load drops from a hundred and ten to sixty pounds, which tells you how much of the standard version's weight came from the short range.

Hits: Glutes and quads through a longer range than the standard version, hamstrings and traps assisting.

Purpose: Getting range back into a movement whose main limitation is that the bar runs out of room. Same idea as the deficit barbell row in ABC+D1.

Swap with: Behind the back deadlift from the floor. Barbell hack squat from a deficit. Conventional deficit deadlift if the bar position is awkward.

Watch: Deficits increase both range and risk. Keep the load conservative and the back position fixed, and make sure the platform is stable.

hip_thruster_hip_thruster_p_glute_builde.html:
Shoulders on a bench or in a dedicated Glute Builder frame, bar across the hips, driving the hips up to full extension. Twenty-four logged sessions across ABCD11 and all three of your own blocks, at up to two hundred and fifty pounds. It is the only movement in the atlas where the glute is the primary target rather than an assistant, and it loads the muscle at its shortest position, which squats and presses never reach.

Hits: Gluteus maximus at full contraction, with the hamstrings assisting and the quads holding the shin angle. No spinal load at all when set up correctly.

Purpose: Direct glute loading. Every squat and press in this atlas trains the glute in its lengthened range; nothing else trains it shortened, which is why this movement earns its own slot rather than being folded into leg day's squatting.

Swap with: Barbell hip thrust off a plain bench if there is no frame. Single leg hip thrust for unilateral work. Cable pull-through or 45-degree back extension for hip extension with less setup.

Watch: Over-extending at the top by arching the lower back instead of finishing with the glutes — tuck the ribs down and stop when the hips are level with the knees and shoulders. Use a pad on the bar.

cadeira_abdutora.html:
Seated, pushing the knees apart against resistance. It trains the gluteus medius on the side of the hip, which is a different muscle from the gluteus maximus and has a different job: it stops the pelvis dropping and the knee caving inward when you stand on one leg. Nothing else in the atlas trains it directly.

Hits: Gluteus medius primarily, with the upper fibres of the gluteus maximus assisting.

Purpose: Hip stability. A weak gluteus medius is one of the common reasons knees cave in during squats and lunges, so this is a cheap insurance movement rather than a size one.

Swap with: Banded lateral walks or clamshells for the same target with no machine. Single leg hip thrust, which demands medius stability as a side effect. Bulgarian split squats done strictly.

Watch: Leaning back and using momentum with a heavy stack. The gluteus medius is a small muscle; high reps at moderate load beat two hundred and fifty-five pounds of bouncing.

calves_leg_press_panturrilha_press.html:
Pressing through the balls of the feet on a leg press platform with the legs nearly locked. Twenty-one logged sessions and ten programs makes this by far your most-used calf movement, and the three hundred and ninety-pound top load is the second heaviest number in the atlas. The near-straight leg means the gastrocnemius is the target, and the machine's support means you can load it far past what a standing raise allows.

Hits: Gastrocnemius primarily because the knee is nearly straight, with the soleus underneath assisting. Nothing else is involved.

Purpose: Heavy straight-leg calf loading, usually as the last line of leg day at six sets of fifteen. The high set count is deliberate: the calf tolerates and needs more volume than most muscles.

Swap with: Smith machine calf raise standing for the same muscle with a free-weight setup. Standing calf raise machine. Seated calf raise if you want the soleus instead — not a substitute, a complement.

Watch: Short, bouncy partial reps, which is how almost everyone does this movement and why almost nobody's calves grow from it. Let the heel drop for a full stretch, pause, then press all the way up onto the toes.

panturrilha_smith.html:
Standing under the Smith bar with the toes on a block or plate, raising up onto them. Standing loads the calf through the whole body's line rather than through a machine's platform, and the Smith's fixed track means you do not have to balance a heavy bar on your back while up on your toes.

Hits: Gastrocnemius with the leg straight, soleus assisting. Adductors and the whole leg work isometrically to hold you upright.

Purpose: Standing calf work when no dedicated standing machine exists, which is most gyms.

Swap with: Calf press on leg press for more load with less balance. Standing calf raise machine. Single leg calf raise holding a dumbbell for a bodyweight alternative.

Watch: The block being too thin to allow a real stretch at the bottom. Use something high enough that the heel can drop well below the toes.

calves_on_glutebuilder_p_toes_inward_p.en: Calves on Glute Builder, Toes Inward
calves_on_glutebuilder_p_toes_inward_p.html:
A calf raise done in the Glute Builder frame with the toes turned inward. Foot rotation does change the emphasis between the two heads of the gastrocnemius — toes in biases the outer head, toes out the inner — though the effect is smaller than the internet claims. Its real value here is having a second calf movement with a different setup, in the two blocks that also ran the Smith raise.

Hits: Gastrocnemius with a modest bias toward the lateral head, soleus assisting.

Purpose: A second calf angle. When a muscle responds to volume as well as the calf does, two movements at different foot positions is a reasonable way to spend the sets.

Swap with: Calf press with toes inward on the leg press, which is the same idea. Smith machine calf raise with a rotated foot position. Standing calf raise.

Watch: Forcing the foot rotation from the ankle rather than the hip. Turn the whole leg slightly rather than twisting the knee.

panturrilha_sentado.html:
Prescribed in ABC01 at six sets of fifteen to close leg day, and once more after that. The bent knee slackens the gastrocnemius and hands the work to the soleus underneath — which is the larger of the two muscles by cross-section and contributes most of the calf's standing endurance. That it never appears in your logs means the soleus has been the least trained muscle in this atlas for two years.

Hits: Soleus primarily, gastrocnemius minimally because of the knee angle.

Purpose: The soleus, which no other movement here trains. Its absence is the clearest gap the data reveals.

Swap with: Bent-knee calf raise on a leg press with the knees deliberately flexed. Smith machine seated calf raise with the bar across the knees. Standing calf raise with a bent knee as the crude version. Note that no straight-leg movement substitutes for this.

Watch: Short range, as with every calf movement. Full stretch at the bottom, full contraction at the top, and higher reps than you think — the soleus is built almost entirely of slow-twitch fibre.

abdominal_crunch.html:
The most-logged movement in your entire history at fifty-six sessions. A short-range curl of the ribs toward the pelvis with the lower back staying on the floor. Its value is not the load — there is none — but that it trains spinal flexion directly with no setup and no risk, which is why it survives in a program that also has dragon flags and cable crunches.

Hits: Upper rectus abdominis primarily, since the movement is the ribcage travelling toward a fixed pelvis, with the obliques assisting.

Purpose: Baseline trunk flexion volume. In four of the five programs it appears in, it is one of several ab lines rather than the only one — the others cover the jobs it does not.

Swap with: Cable crunch if you want the movement loaded, which is the main thing a bodyweight crunch lacks. Bosu ball weighted crunch for range plus load. Weighted sit-ups.

Watch: Pulling on the neck with the hands and turning it into a hip flexor movement by coming all the way up. Keep the lower back down and the range short.

weighted_crunches_p_bosu_ball_p.html:
Lying back over a Bosu ball with a weight held at the chest. The ball lets the spine extend backward past flat before the crunch begins, which roughly doubles the working range of a normal crunch, and the weight means the movement can actually be progressed. Twenty-eight sessions and a hundred and four sets makes this the most heavily used loaded ab movement in the atlas.

Hits: Rectus abdominis through a much longer range than a floor crunch, upper and lower portions together, with the obliques stabilising on the unstable surface.

Purpose: Loaded, full-range spinal flexion. It solves both of the plain crunch's problems — no load and no range — in one movement.

Swap with: Cable crunch kneeling for a similar loaded flexion with a different resistance curve. Crunch on a stability ball if no Bosu. Decline weighted sit-ups.

Watch: Extending too far back over the ball under load, which puts a real stretch on the lumbar spine. Let the range build over weeks rather than chasing it in week one.

abdominal_na_polia_alta.html:
Kneeling below a high pulley, curling the torso down against the cable. Ten of nineteen programs prescribe it, more than any other ab movement, and the reason is simple: it is the only conventional ab exercise that can be progressively loaded like any other lift. The abs respond to progressive overload the same as every other muscle, and bodyweight crunches cannot provide it.

Hits: Rectus abdominis through flexion under genuine resistance, with the obliques assisting and the lats working isometrically to hold the rope.

Purpose: Progressive overload for the abs. It is the ab movement you track a number on.

Swap with: Bosu ball weighted crunch for more range. Machine crunch if the cable setup is awkward. Weighted sit-ups as the low-tech version.

Watch: Turning it into a hip hinge by bowing at the waist rather than curling the spine. The hips should stay fixed and the movement should come entirely from rounding the back — think of bringing the ribs to the knees.

abdominal_remador.html:
Sitting and bringing the knees and chest together at the same time, like the recovery of a rowing stroke. Combining trunk flexion with hip flexion means the abs work from both ends simultaneously, which reaches the lower portion of the rectus that a plain crunch leaves out. Four programs run it, usually bi-set with a plank.

Hits: The full length of the rectus abdominis, upper and lower together, with the hip flexors doing real work and the obliques stabilising.

Purpose: Covering both ends of the rectus in one movement, which is efficient when a program only has one or two ab slots.

Swap with: Weighted rower crunch to load it. V-ups or jackknife crunches, which are the same pattern. Hanging leg raises if you want the lower abs with more range.

Watch: Rocking on the tailbone to generate momentum. Each rep should start from a controlled extended position, not from a bounce.

abdominal_remador_weighted.html:
The rower crunch with a weight held at the chest, opening ABC+D1's push day at four sets of twenty. Six pounds sounds trivial until you do twenty reps of a movement where the abs are working from both ends — the load is correctly small because the leverage is already long.

Hits: Full rectus abdominis with added resistance, hip flexors and obliques assisting.

Purpose: Progressing the rower crunch, and putting abs first in the session so they actually get done. Eighteen sessions says the placement worked.

Swap with: Rower crunch unloaded. Weighted V-ups. Cable crunch if you want heavier loading with less hip involvement.

Watch: The weight pulling you into a rock rather than a curl. Keep it at the chest, not overhead.

abdominal_supra_bracos_esticados_p_com_p.html:
A crunch with the arms held straight overhead holding a weight, which moves the load as far from the hip as possible and makes the lever enormous. Seventeen and a half pounds held overhead is harder than double that held at the chest, which is the entire principle: you do not need heavy weight to make abs work hard, you need a long lever.

Hits: Upper rectus abdominis, with the lats and front delts working isometrically to keep the arms locked overhead.

Purpose: Loading the abs through leverage rather than weight, which keeps the spine's compressive load low while the muscular demand goes up.

Swap with: Crunch with the arms straight and no weight. Long lever plank for the anti-extension version of the same principle. Cable crunch for load.

Watch: The arms drifting forward as the set gets hard, which shortens the lever and makes it a normal crunch. Keep them beside the ears.

weighted_sit_ups.html:
A full sit-up with a weight at the chest, closing ABCD09's upper day. Unlike a crunch, a sit-up continues past the point where the spine has finished flexing, at which point the hip flexors take over and lift the whole torso — which is why sit-ups are as much a hip flexor movement as an ab one.

Hits: Rectus abdominis through the first portion and the hip flexors through the rest.

Purpose: Loaded trunk flexion with no equipment beyond a plate. A reasonable finisher.

Swap with: Cable crunch for more isolated ab loading. Bosu ball weighted crunch for range. Butterfly sit-ups for the hip-flexor-reduced version.

Watch: The lower back arching off the floor at the start of each rep and the hands pulling the head forward. If the hip flexors are what you feel, shorten the range into a crunch.

abdominal_crossfit.html:
A sit-up with the legs splayed open in a butterfly position rather than bent in front. Opening the hips puts the hip flexors in a disadvantaged position, so more of the work has to come from the abs themselves — which is a neat fix for the main criticism of the sit-up.

Hits: Rectus abdominis with less hip flexor contribution than a standard sit-up, obliques assisting.

Purpose: A sit-up that is actually an ab exercise. High-rep conditioning work.

Swap with: Weighted sit-ups if you want load. Crunch for the shorter, safer range. Rower crunch.

Watch: The open-hip position can be uncomfortable for tight hips. Also resist using arm swing for momentum.

abdomen_infra_no_solo.html:
Lying on the floor, raising straight legs. Thirty-two logged sessions makes this your second most-used ab movement. Critically, ABC04 moved leg raises to the first line of the day at five sets of twelve to fifteen — the fix for abs having been skipped for three programs running. Putting them first is why they have thirty-two sessions and not five.

Hits: Lower rectus abdominis, but only if the pelvis actually tilts at the top — otherwise it is purely hip flexor work with the abs holding still.

Purpose: The lower abs, which crunches barely touch because the pelvis stays fixed in a crunch and moves in a leg raise.

Swap with: Hanging leg raises for far more range and difficulty. Bench leg raises to get below horizontal. Weighted reverse crunch for the loaded version.

Watch: The lower back arching off the floor as the legs come down, which is where people hurt themselves. Press the lower back into the floor and shorten the range rather than letting it lift. Curl the hips slightly at the top to actually involve the abs.

abdomen_infra_no_banco.html:
Lying on a bench with the legs hanging off the end, so they can drop below horizontal before coming up. That extra range at the bottom is the whole reason to use a bench, and it makes the movement considerably harder than the floor version because the abs have to control a longer lever from a stretched position.

Hits: Lower rectus abdominis through a longer range, with the hip flexors assisting.

Purpose: Extending the range of the leg raise without needing a pull-up bar to hang from.

Swap with: Incline bench leg raises for more difficulty. Hanging leg raises. Leg raises on the floor if the lower back objects.

Watch: The same lower-back arch as the floor version, made worse by the extra range. Hold the bench behind your head and keep the pelvis tucked.

abdominal_infra_no_banco_inclinado.html:
Leg raises on a decline bench with the head higher than the hips, so gravity acts against the legs through a longer portion of the arc than on a flat bench. It is the hardest unloaded leg raise variation in the atlas and appears in five programs.

Hits: Lower rectus abdominis with a longer resistance curve, hip flexors and obliques assisting.

Purpose: Progressing the leg raise by angle rather than by adding weight, which keeps the movement clean.

Swap with: Bench leg raises flat if the incline is too much. Hanging leg raises. Weighted reverse crunch.

Watch: Grip on the bench above your head taking over, and the pelvis failing to tuck at the top. Slow the descent rather than adding reps.

abdominal_infra_no_banco_p_com_peso_p.html:
A reverse crunch — curling the pelvis toward the ribs rather than the ribs toward the pelvis — with a small weight between the feet. Nineteen sessions in ABC+D1. The reverse direction is what makes this specifically a lower-ab movement: the pelvis is what moves, and pelvic tilt is the lower rectus's actual job.

Hits: Lower rectus abdominis through posterior pelvic tilt, which is the most direct loading of that portion available. Hip flexors assist.

Purpose: Loading the lower abs specifically. Three pounds is the right order of magnitude — the leverage does the work.

Swap with: Leg raises with a deliberate hip curl at the top. Hanging knee raises with a pelvic tuck. Incline bench leg raises.

Watch: Making it a leg raise by swinging the legs rather than curling the hips. The knees can stay bent; what matters is the pelvis rolling.

abdominal_canivete.html:
Starting flat and folding in the middle so the hands and feet meet above the hips — the same idea as a V-up. Both ends of the body travel at once, which makes the abs work through their whole length against the longest possible lever.

Hits: Full rectus abdominis, hip flexors doing substantial work, obliques stabilising.

Purpose: Maximum-leverage bodyweight ab work. When a program wants abs to be genuinely difficult without adding load, this is the answer.

Swap with: Rower crunch, which is nearly the same movement from a seated start. V-ups. Dragon flag if you want the hardest version of this family.

Watch: Bouncing off the floor between reps. Each rep should start from a controlled hollow position, not a rebound.

dragon_flag.html:
Lying on a bench holding behind your head, the whole body lifted and lowered as a rigid plank pivoting at the shoulders. Bruce Lee's movement, and the hardest thing in this section by a wide margin — the abs have to hold the entire body straight while gravity tries to fold it. Twenty-six sessions with only twenty-nine working sets tells the story: roughly one set per session, because one set is what you get.

Hits: The full rectus abdominis working isometrically to prevent the spine extending, with the obliques, lats and hip flexors all recruited to hold the line. It trains the trunk's bracing function rather than its curling function.

Purpose: Anti-extension strength at the highest difficulty available without equipment. This is the quality that transfers to holding position under a heavy bar, which a crunch does not.

Swap with: Ab wheel rollout for the same anti-extension quality at a manageable difficulty. Hanging leg raise with a straight body. Long lever plank as the static regression. Tuck dragon flag as the direct progression step.

Watch: The lower back arching as you lower, which is the point at which the movement becomes dangerous rather than hard. Bend the knees to shorten the lever until you can keep the body rigid, and stop the set the moment the hips sag.

abdominal_com_carrinho.html:
Rolling out from the knees and back, with the abs resisting the spine being pulled into an arch. Twenty sessions at exactly one set each — the same signature as the dragon flag, and for the same reason. The further you roll, the longer the lever and the harder the abs have to work to stop your hips dropping.

Hits: Rectus abdominis isometrically through a long lever, with the lats and front delts controlling the roll and the obliques preventing any twist.

Purpose: Anti-extension with an adjustable difficulty — you set the load by how far you roll, which makes it far more scalable than a dragon flag.

Swap with: Dragon flag for a harder version. Plank for the static regression. Barbell rollout if there is no wheel. Body saw on sliders.

Watch: Letting the lower back arch at full extension, which is the standard failure and is exactly what the movement is supposed to prevent. Roll only as far as you can keep the ribs tucked, and add distance over weeks.

prancha.html:
The static hold, prescribed in ABC01 as four sets of thirty to forty seconds bi-set with the rower crunch. Pairing a static anti-extension hold with a dynamic flexion movement in one bi-set is a tidy piece of programming — two of the trunk's three jobs in a single line.

Hits: Rectus abdominis isometrically, with the obliques, glutes and front delts all contributing to holding the line.

Purpose: Teaching and training the braced position. It is the entry point to anti-extension work and the regression for everything else in this group.

Swap with: Ab wheel for the dynamic version. Long lever plank with the elbows further forward if thirty seconds is easy. Plank on ball.

Watch: Hips sagging or riding high, and holding for time long past the point where the position has degraded. Thirty good seconds beats ninety bad ones; squeeze the glutes and tuck the ribs.

prancha_na_bola.html:
A plank with the forearms on a stability ball. The instability means the trunk is not just resisting extension but constantly correcting small wobbles in every direction, which recruits the obliques and the serratus far more than a floor plank does.

Hits: Rectus abdominis plus significantly more oblique and serratus work than a static floor plank, with the front delts stabilising the shoulder.

Purpose: Making a plank hard again without adding time. It also trains the serratus, which matters for overhead shoulder health and which almost nothing else in this atlas touches.

Swap with: Plank on the floor if the ball is too much. Ab wheel for a dynamic alternative. Stir-the-pot on the ball for a progression.

Watch: The hips sagging while you concentrate on the wobble. The position rules from the plain plank still apply.

escalador_alternado.html:
A plank position with the knees driving alternately toward the chest. Prescribed once. It combines the anti-extension demand of a plank with alternating hip flexion, and the alternation adds a mild anti-rotation element as each leg moves.

Hits: Rectus abdominis holding the plank, hip flexors driving the knees, obliques resisting rotation, front delts supporting.

Purpose: Conditioning as much as abs. It is the one movement in this section with a real cardiovascular component.

Swap with: Plank for the pure hold. Rower crunch for the hip flexion. Ab wheel if strength rather than conditioning is the goal.

Watch: The hips rising into a pike as the pace picks up. Speed is not the point; holding the plank while the legs move is.

abdominal_obliquo.html:
A crunch angled to one side, or performed lying on the side, so the torso bends laterally rather than straight forward. Twenty sessions across five programs. Side flexion is one of the obliques' two jobs and it is the one nothing else in the section trains — cross crunches cover rotation, this covers bending.

Hits: Obliques through lateral flexion, with the rectus abdominis assisting.

Purpose: The side of the trunk. In a programme whose other ab work is all forward flexion and bracing, this is the lateral plane.

Swap with: Side plank for the isometric version of the same plane. Dumbbell side bend if you want it loaded. Cross crunch for rotation instead.

Watch: Yanking on the neck. Keep the range short and the movement coming from the ribcage, not the arms.

abdominal_cruzado.html:
A crunch that brings one elbow toward the opposite knee, so the trunk rotates as it flexes. Rotation is the obliques' primary function — they run diagonally across the abdomen precisely so they can twist the ribcage against the pelvis — and a straight crunch cannot train it at all.

Hits: Obliques through rotation, with the rectus abdominis contributing the flexion component.

Purpose: Rotational trunk work. Nineteen sessions in a single program means it was doing a job nothing else in that program did.

Swap with: Side plank with rotation for a harder version. Ball torso rotation for standing rotation. Russian twist or cable woodchop for loaded rotation.

Watch: Rotating from the neck rather than the ribcage. The shoulder should travel across, and the elbow reaching the knee is a result, not a target.

prancha_lateral_com_rotacao.html:
Holding a side plank and then rotating the torso, threading the top arm under the body and back out. It combines two things nothing else in the section does together: the lateral bracing of a side plank and active rotation under that brace. Thirteen sessions across four programs.

Hits: Obliques as the clear primary, doing both of their jobs at once, with the rectus abdominis, glutes and front delt holding the side-plank position.

Purpose: The most complete oblique movement in the atlas — lateral stability plus rotation in one rep. It is also the only one where the glutes contribute meaningfully.

Swap with: Side plank static for the regression. Cross crunch for rotation lying down. Pallof press for anti-rotation under load.

Watch: The hips dropping during the rotation, which is when the movement stops training the brace. Keep the bottom hip lifted throughout.

rotacao_de_tronco_com_bola.html:
Standing or kneeling, rotating a medicine ball from side to side. Standing rotation is a different pattern from lying rotation because the pelvis is free to move, so the movement has to be controlled by the trunk deciding how much of the rotation comes from the hips and how much from the ribcage.

Hits: Obliques through rotation, with the rectus abdominis and erectors working together to keep the spine stacked while it turns.
