Purpose: Rotation in a standing position, which is closer to how the trunk actually gets used than any lying variation. Usually prescribed as a warm-up or a finisher.

Swap with: Cable woodchop for a loaded, better-resisted version. Russian twist seated. Landmine rotation. Cross crunch if a ball is not available.

Watch: Swinging from the arms and letting the lower back do the twisting. Rotation should come from the ribcage turning over a stable pelvis.

rotacao_externa_ombro.html:
Elbow at the side, forearm rotating outward against light resistance. It arrived in ABC04 along with its internal counterpart and never left — sixteen of the nineteen programs since, always at the very top of the day, one set of ten at six pounds. The timing of its arrival is the interesting part: ABC04 was the realization block where reps dropped to six to eight and the loads went up. Heavy pressing at six reps is exactly where shoulders start to complain, and the rotations appearing in that same block is not a coincidence.

Hits: The infraspinatus and teres minor — two of the four rotator cuff muscles — with the rear delt assisting. These sit behind the shoulder blade and their job is holding the ball of the arm centred in the socket while the big muscles move it.

Purpose: Keeping the shoulder joint tracking properly under heavy pressing. It builds nothing visible and prevents the single most common injury in this kind of training. Six pounds for ten reps costs ninety seconds and is the highest return per minute in the atlas.

Swap with: Cable external rotation for constant tension. Band external rotation, which is the most convenient version. Face pulls cover the same muscles as part of a bigger movement. Side-lying dumbbell external rotation.

Watch: Using any real weight. The cuff muscles are small and the moment you go heavy enough that the shoulder or the lats start helping, the exercise has stopped working. Six pounds is correct. Keep the elbow pinned to the side.

rotacao_interna_ombro.html:
The most-logged movement in this atlas after the crunch, and the partner to the external rotation — the two always appear together, one set of ten each, at the top of the day. This one trains the subscapularis, the cuff muscle on the front of the shoulder blade, which is the largest and strongest of the four and the one most often left out of prehab routines because people assume pressing covers it.

Hits: Subscapularis primarily, with the front delt and lat assisting. It sits on the inside face of the shoulder blade, which is why no diagram can show it properly — the figure here marks the cuff region generally.

Purpose: Completing the cuff. Training only external rotation leaves an imbalance; doing both keeps the joint centred in every direction. Together with the external rotation this is the pair that has appeared in sixteen consecutive programs.

Swap with: Cable internal rotation. Band internal rotation. Side-lying internal rotation with a light dumbbell. Dumbbell circles as broader shoulder prep, though it is less specific.

Watch: The same rule as its partner — the load stays light forever. Elbow at the side, forearm rotating across the body, no torso movement.

pectoralis-major.png.name: Pectoralis major
pectoralis-major.png.text: Pulls the upper arm across the body and forward. The upper (clavicular) portion runs from the collarbone and needs the arm to travel up as well as in — the whole reason incline pressing exists as its own category. The larger lower portion runs from the breastbone.

serratus-anterior.png.name: Serratus anterior
serratus-anterior.png.text: The finger-like muscle over the ribs. It pulls the shoulder blade forward and around the ribcage, which is what lets you reach overhead without the shoulder pinching. Trained best by pullovers and ball planks.

latissimus-dorsi.png.name: Latissimus dorsi
latissimus-dorsi.png.text: The big fan across the back. Pulls the upper arm down and back toward the ribs — which is why both pulldowns and rows train it, through different paths. Builds width.

trapezius.png.name: Trapezius
trapezius.png.text: Three regions in one muscle. The upper portion shrugs, the middle pulls the shoulder blades together, the lower pulls them down. Upright rows hit the upper, rows hit the middle.

rhomboid.png.name: Rhomboids
rhomboid.png.text: Sits between the shoulder blades and squeezes them together. A row that stops short of the squeeze trains far less of this than you think. Builds thickness, not width.

teres-major.png.name: Teres major
teres-major.png.text: A small muscle under the armpit that assists the lat in pulling the arm down and back, working alongside it on every row and pulldown.

erector-spinae.png.name: Erector spinae
erector-spinae.png.text: Runs either side of the spine. Its job is stopping your back from rounding, so it works hardest on movements where nothing is holding your torso up — bent-over rows, good mornings, deadlifts.

deltoid.png.name: Deltoid
deltoid.png.text: Three muscles sharing a name. The front head presses overhead and gets worked by every chest press. The side head lifts the arm out sideways and is trained almost only by raises. The rear head pulls the arm backward and is functionally a back muscle.

infraspinatus.png.name: Infraspinatus
infraspinatus.png.text: One of the four rotator cuff muscles, on the back of the shoulder blade. Rotates the arm outward and keeps the ball of the arm centred in the socket. This is what external rotations train.

subscapularis.png.name: Subscapularis
subscapularis.png.text: The largest rotator cuff muscle, on the inside face of the shoulder blade. Rotates the arm inward. Most often left out of prehab routines because people assume pressing covers it.

biceps-brachii.png.name: Biceps brachii
biceps-brachii.png.text: Bends the elbow and rotates the palm upward. It also crosses the shoulder, which is why the position of your upper arm — behind you on an incline curl, in front on a preacher curl — changes which part of the range is hardest.

brachialis.png.name: Brachialis
brachialis.png.text: Sits underneath and slightly outside the biceps. Bends the elbow but does not rotate the forearm, so a neutral grip loads it more. Training it adds width to the upper arm.

triceps-brachii.png.name: Triceps brachii
triceps-brachii.png.text: Straightens the elbow. The long head also crosses the shoulder, so overhead extensions load a part of it that pushdowns barely touch — which is why programs pair one of each.

forearm-flexors.png.name: Forearm flexors
forearm-flexors.png.text: Bend the wrist and curl the fingers. The deep finger flexors are what actually fail when a heavy row or deadlift slips out of your hands.

forearm-extensors.png.name: Forearm extensors
forearm-extensors.png.text: Straighten the wrist and fingers on the back of the forearm. Work isometrically on every heavy pull to keep the wrist from collapsing.

rectus-abdominis.png.name: Rectus abdominis
rectus-abdominis.png.text: Curls the ribcage toward the pelvis. It also works isometrically to stop the spine being pulled into an arch — a completely different quality, and what planks, ab wheels and dragon flags train.

obliques.png.name: Obliques
obliques.png.text: Run diagonally across the abdomen so they can rotate and side-bend the torso. A straight crunch cannot train rotation at all.

gluteus-maximus.png.name: Gluteus maximus
gluteus-maximus.png.text: Extends the hip. Every squat and press trains it in its lengthened range; only a hip thrust loads it fully shortened, which is why that movement earns its own slot.

gluteus-medius.png.name: Gluteus medius
gluteus-medius.png.text: On the side of the hip. Stops the pelvis dropping and the knee caving inward when you stand on one leg. Weakness here is a common reason knees cave during squats and lunges.

quadriceps.png.name: Quadriceps
quadriceps.png.text: Four muscles that straighten the knee. How upright your torso is decides how much of the work they take versus the hips — which is the whole point of hack squats and Smith squats.

rectus-femoris.png.name: Rectus femoris
rectus-femoris.png.text: The only quad muscle that crosses the hip, so it is fully loaded only when the hip is extended. Squats and leg presses under-train it; sissy squats and reclined leg extensions are the fix.

vastus-lateralis.png.name: Vastus lateralis
vastus-lateralis.png.text: The outer quad, the largest of the four. Gets the most work from squats and presses with the feet placed low and narrow.

vastus-medialis.png.name: Vastus medialis
vastus-medialis.png.text: The inner quad just above the knee. Works hardest through the last part of knee extension, which is why full lockout matters.

adductor-magnus.jpg.name: Adductors
adductor-magnus.jpg.text: Pull the thigh inward. Get far more work than people expect from any wide-stance squat or deep lunge.

biceps-femoris.png.name: Hamstrings
biceps-femoris.png.text: Bend the knee and also extend the hip. Doing two jobs is why leg curls and Romanian deadlifts both count as hamstring work but are not interchangeable.

gastrocnemius.png.name: Gastrocnemius
gastrocnemius.png.text: The visible diamond-shaped calf muscle. It crosses the knee as well as the ankle, so it works best with the leg straight. Beneath it the soleus does the same job with the knee bent — the whole argument for seated calf raises.

tibialis-anterior.png.name: Tibialis anterior
tibialis-anterior.png.text: On the front of the shin. Pulls the foot upward. Rarely trained directly but works on every lunge and walk.
